docs.title: papers
docs.text:
Command-line tool to manage your bibliography (PDFs + BibTeX).

papers keeps a BibTeX file for each of your projects, and the PDFs that go with it. Give it a PDF: it reads the DOI, fetches the entry from crossref, renames the PDF after the entry and adds both to your project. A project can use another library as its pool, and take its entries and PDFs from there, so that each PDF is stored and fetched once.

It works like git: one papers command with subcommands, run inside a project folder.

  • Add papers from PDFs, DOIs, bibtex, RIS, CSL-JSON or BibJSON files, or whole folders. The DOI is read from the PDF, and the metadata comes from crossref (by DOI or full-text search), doi.org, google scholar or OpenAlex.
  • Name the PDFs with a template ({authorX}_{year}_{title} by default), and attach supplements to an entry.
  • Share entries and PDFs between projects: a shallow project uses another library as its pool, takes its entries from there and links to its PDFs; any library can also exchange entries with another one (--pool PATH). papers pull, push and sync exchange the entries with a field-by-field three-way merge; each project keeps its own keys.
  • Search and act on a library with papers list (tag, edit, delete, rename, fetch, deduplicate), in the style of find and grep.
  • Detect duplicates by DOI, arXiv identifier, ISBN, or authors and title, and merge them.
  • Export a selection as a library with copies of its PDFs, or as RIS and CSL-JSON (for Zotero, EndNote, pandoc) or BibJSON (for programs).
  • Plain files: the bibtex is the database, the PDFs stay in folders you see, and the library can be edited with any tool.
  • Undo anything: every command is a step of the library's history, kept on your computer; papers undo / papers redo take back any command, with the files it moved, renamed or deleted, and a change made outside papers is never lost.
  • Fast on large libraries: the parsed bibtex is cached piece by piece, and papers status compares a project with its pool only where they changed.

docs.title: Adding entries
docs.text: The papers add command adds entries to your library, with or without a PDF attachment.

docs.title: Add a PDF (extract metadata automatically)
docs.text:
$> papers add esd-4-11-2013.pdf --bibtex papers.bib --filesdir files -v
papers: info: found doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013
papers: info: new entry: perrette_landerer2013
papers: info: mv /home/perrette/playground/papers/esd-4-11-2013.pdf files/perrette_et_al_2013_a-scaling-approach-to-project-regional-sea-level-rise-and-its-uncertainties.pdf
papers: info: renamed file(s): 1

That is equivalent to doing:

papers extract esd-4-11-2013.pdf > entry.bib
papers add entry.bib --attach esd-4-11-2013.pdf --bibtex papers.bib --filesdir files

docs.title: How the DOI is found
docs.text:
papers add looks for the DOI of a PDF in this order:

  1. The PDF metadata: the subject, keywords and title fields of the document information, then the XMP tags prism:doi, dc:identifier (doi:...), pdfx:doi and crossmark:DOI. A DOI found there is used as is.
  2. The text of the first pages: pages are read one at a time until there are 200 words (at most 10 pages). A DOI is 10., 4 to 9 digits, /, then letters, digits and -._;()/:, not glued to a preceding word (case is ignored). A DOI broken over two lines after 10. or after a dash is joined, and trailing text such as .pdf, supplement or an unbalanced ) is cut. If the PDF has more than one page, the DOIs of the last page that follow doi: or doi.org/ are added after those of the first pages (some publishers append a cover page).
  3. The candidates are ordered: a DOI written in a doi.org URL first, then the others in order of appearance; the DOIs of data repositories (Zenodo, Dryad, figshare, PANGAEA...) come last, and a supplement DOI (ending in .s1) after the DOI of the article. Each candidate is fetched (from crossref), and the first one whose title appears in the first pages (ignoring case, accents and punctuation) is used. This skips the DOIs of cited papers.
  4. If the text has no DOI, an arXiv identifier written arXiv:2101.01234 gives the DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2101.01234, whose metadata come from arXiv and are checked as in step 3.

When no DOI is accepted, papers searches crossref with the first 200 words of the text (--scholar: Google Scholar, --openalex: OpenAlex, see below), and accepts the result only if its title appears in the text. Otherwise the PDF is not added, and papers stops with an error: pass the DOI with --doi, or describe the entry (see below). --no-query-doi skips the DOI search, and --no-query-fulltext the text search.

docs.title: Search with OpenAlex
docs.text:
--openalex (of add, extract and fetch) searches OpenAlex instead of crossref: an open catalogue (CC0 data) with an API, where --scholar scrapes the web pages of Google Scholar, which often blocks it. OpenAlex finds the works whose title and abstract are closest in meaning to the text (the first 1500 characters of the query), and papers takes the one that scores best, as for crossref, among those whose title (of at least 20 letters and digits) is in the text, the published works before their preprints. The entry is that of the DOI of the work (crossref, doi.org, arXiv); a work without DOI gives an entry made of its OpenAlex record, with the OpenAlex id as key.

Without a key, OpenAlex allows about 100 searches a day (for all the users of a network). A free key, from openalex.org/settings/api, gives ten times as many: papers reads it from the environment variable OPENALEX_API_KEY. PAPERS_MAILTO, if set, is the email address that OpenAlex is given to identify the requests. Searches are at most one a second, and are saved in the cache (see Configuration).

papers extract --doi-only FILE prints the DOI that steps 1 to 4 find, without adding anything:

$ papers extract --doi-only bg-8-515-2011.pdf
10.5194/bg-8-515-2011

docs.title: What happens to the files
docs.text:
By default, papers add moves the PDF into the files directory of the library, under a name made from the name template: in a shallow library (a library with a pool), the files directory and the name template of its pool (see Shallow libraries). The files setting of the library changes what happens to the original (see Files):

  • move (default): place the file in the files directory and remove the original;
  • copy: place it in the files directory and keep the original (a hard link when possible, otherwise a copy);
  • link: leave it where it is; the entry links to it there;
  • ask: ask for each file, m (move), c (copy) or l (link, also Enter); M, C or L answers for all the next files; without a terminal, the file is linked where it is.

--move, --copy and --link override the setting for one command (-r/--rename is the same as --move, -c as --copy):

papers config files copy           # this library keeps the originals
papers add esd-4-11-2013.pdf --link

A file that belongs to another library (inside its files directory) is never moved: it is copied instead, so that the other library keeps its link.

The same applies to the files linked from the entries of a bibtex file added with papers add other.bib: their paths are read relative to that bibtex, and when they are linked where they are (link), they are stored so that they remain valid from your own bibtex (relative to it, or absolute, according to the paths setting of the library).

See Renaming files and keys for how to specify file naming patterns, and how the files of an entry with attachments are named.

docs.title: Attach files
docs.text:
--attach FILE... attaches other files to the added entry (e.g. supplementary material), placed as the files setting says. They are named after the main file (see Renaming files and keys). To attach files to an entry already in the library, use papers file attach KEY FILE.... --attachment is a deprecated name of --attach.

-a is the short form of --author (as in papers list). In papers v2, -a FILE... attached files: until v4, when every value given to -a is an existing file (or a URL), papers attaches them as with --attach and warns. Otherwise the first value is the author, and the next values are files to add (papers add -a "Smith, John" paper.pdf); a first value that is an existing file, followed by other values, is an error.

docs.title: Add a whole directory of PDFs
docs.text:
It is possible to do this on a full directory of files, recursively, with -R/--recursive:

papers add -R /home/perette/playground/papers/papers_test

where, above, the papers_test directory contains a few PDF files. For each PDF, papers will attempt to extract the metadata and add the relevant file to the bibliography, and place the files as the files setting says (by default, moved into the files directory).

Files named after a PDF of the same directory, as papers names attachments (<name>--<label>.<ext> next to <name>.pdf, see Renaming files and keys), are added as attachments of that PDF's entry, whatever their type, instead of being scanned as papers of their own. Bibtex files found in the directory are added too, before the PDFs, and the files they link to are not scanned: their entry comes from the bibtex, so a folder that holds a bibtex and its files is added without looking anything up online. Folders of the pre-2.19 layout (with a hidden .<name>.bib) are read from their hidden bibtex.

The metadata of each PDF are found as for a single PDF (see How the DOI is found). If none matches, the PDF is not added: pass its DOI with --doi (see below), or, for a reference without DOI (older papers, books, reports...), describe it and attach the PDF:

papers add --title "Self-consistent equilibrium ocean tides" --author "Agnew, Duncan C. and Farrell, W. E." \
    --year 1978 --journal "Geophysical Journal International" --attach agnew1978.pdf

docs.title: Entries already in the library
docs.text:
When the DOI of the added paper is already in the library (given with --doi, or found in the PDF metadata, or printed in the text of the PDF with the title of the library entry), papers add uses that entry: nothing is fetched online and there is no duplicate dialogue. The PDF (and the files of --attach) are attached to the entry and placed as the files setting says, as papers file attach KEY FILE... does; the key, the fields and the other files of the entry are not touched. A file with the content of a file of the entry is not attached again, and stays where it is. An arXiv DOI (10.48550/arXiv.<id>) matches an entry whose eprint is that arXiv identifier. --no-check-duplicate skips this, and adds a new entry.

The order is: the library, then the pool (below), then online.

docs.title: Entries already in the pool
docs.text:
Before querying crossref, papers add looks in the pool of the library (see Pools): a PDF with the same content as a pool file, or whose DOI is in the pool, a DOI that a pool entry has, or a bibtex entry that is the same paper as a pool entry, is taken from the pool, with its files. --no-pool skips this. --pool PATH looks in the library PATH instead, in any library: the entry is taken from PATH with its files, its origin is recorded for PATH, and nothing is added to PATH (papers -C PATH add is what adds to PATH).

papers add --key KEY, with no file, DOI or other field, takes the pool entry of key KEY (ignoring case). When the library already has an entry of that key, the files of --attach are attached to it. When neither has it, papers stops with an error and changes nothing:

papers add --key yool2011

In a shallow library, the files of the added entries go to the files directory of the pool, and the entries to the pool too (see Shallow libraries).

papers add other.bib copies the entries of other.bib once, with no memory of the source. To take entries from the pool so that they stay linked to it (later pulls bring the corrections made there), use papers pull KEY (see papers pull).

docs.title: Add RIS, CSL-JSON and BibJSON files
docs.text:
papers add reads RIS (.ris, as exported by Zotero, EndNote, Web of Science, Scopus...), CSL-JSON (.json, as exported by Zotero or pandoc) and BibJSON (.bib.json, see BibJSON) files, recognized by their extension; --format ris|csl-json|bibjson|bibtex sets the format of a file of another extension. Other files are read as bibtex. RIS needs the rispy package (see Installation).

$ papers add ~/refs.ris --on-duplicate keep
Added -> perrette_yool2011: Near-ubiquity of ice-edge blooms in the Arctic (doi:10.5194/bg-8-515-2011)
Modified -> perrette_landerer2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013, file:1)

The entries are added as those of a bibtex file:

  • the duplicate check and --on-duplicate apply;
  • the key is the ID of a RIS record, or the citation-key or id of a CSL-JSON item, when it is a valid bibtex key; otherwise (the item URIs of Zotero, the record numbers of EndNote) it is made from the key template;
  • the file links (RIS L1; in CSL-JSON, a file key or custom.file, which papers writes, since CSL-JSON has no standard field for files) are read relative to the added file and attached as for a bibtex file; links that are not local files (http://, EndNote's internal-pdf://) are left out with a warning;
  • RIS and CSL-JSON hold plain text: &, %, # and _ are escaped for LaTeX (\&...), except in url, doi, file, eprint, isbn, issn, keywords and urldate; BibJSON values are read as they are, since they are bibtex values;
  • keywords (RIS KW, CSL-JSON keyword) are split on , and ; and joined with , (export splits the keywords field on , only);
  • the CSL-JSON container-title (RIS T2, JO...) is the booktitle of a chapter or a conference paper (incollection, inproceedings), the journal of any other type;
  • a date part that is zero or missing ends the date: 2013-00-05 is the year 2013 only;
  • in a shallow library, the new entries go to the pool too;
  • a directory scan (-R) reads PDFs and bibtex files only.

The fields are converted as papers export --format writes them (see How the fields are converted); a few more are read: T1, JO, JF (title, journal), A2 (editors of a chapter, in EndNote exports), N2 (abstract), M3 (type of a report); and in CSL-JSON, genre (the type of a report or thesis). A thesis whose type (RIS M3, CSL-JSON genre) contains master is a mastersthesis, any other a phdthesis. Other fields are ignored.

docs.title: Add an entry from its DOI
docs.text:
If you already know the DOI of a PDF, and don't want to gamble the fulltext search and match, you can indicate it via --doi:

papers add esd-4-11-2013.pdf --doi 10.5194/esd-4-11-2013 --bibtex papers.bib

The add command above also works without any PDF (create a bibtex entry without file attachment):

papers add --doi 10.5194/esd-4-11-2013 --bibtex papers.bib

With --fetch-pdf, papers also downloads the free PDF of the entry and attaches it, as papers file fetch KEY does (see Fetching the free PDF of an entry):

$ papers add --doi 10.5194/esd-4-11-2013 --fetch-pdf
perrette_landerer2013: files/perrette_et_al_2013_a-scaling-approach-to-project-regional-sea-level-rise-and-its-uncertainties.pdf (published version, from esd.copernicus.org)
Added -> perrette_landerer2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013, file:1)

When no PDF is found, the entry is added all the same, and the command exits with status 1 after the error. Without a library, papers fetch --pdf DOI downloads the PDF into the current directory, under the name of its URL (-o FILE names it), as papers fetch DOI prints the bibtex:

$ papers fetch --pdf 10.5194/bg-8-515-2011
bg-8-515-2011.pdf (published version, from bg.copernicus.org)

For programs, --porcelain prints on the standard output one line per DOI or arXiv id, in the order of the arguments (the other messages go to the standard error): downloaded ID VERSION URL FILE (VERSION: published, accepted or submitted; URL: the link of the PDF), then refused-published ID URL for each link of the published version that was refused before an accepted or submitted version was found; exists ID FILE when the file to write exists (it is not replaced; with -o FILE, nothing is downloaded); when no PDF could be downloaded, refused ID URL for each link to open in a browser, or failed ID when there is none (not a DOI or arXiv id). The command exits with status 1 when an argument gave no PDF:

$ papers fetch --pdf 10.5194/bg-8-515-2011 --porcelain 2>/dev/null
downloaded 10.5194/bg-8-515-2011 published https://bg.copernicus.org/articles/8/515/2011/bg-8-515-2011.pdf bg-8-515-2011.pdf

docs.title: Add an entry without DOI from bibtex + PDF
docs.text:
Some old files don't have a DOI. The best approach is to add the entry from its bibtex:

papers add entry.bib --attach esd-4-11-2013.pdf --bibtex papers.bib --filesdir files

docs.title: Set fields on the command line
docs.text:
--title, --author, --year, --journal, --type (the entry type, e.g. book), --key and --metadata KEY=VALUE... (any field) set these fields of the added entry. They replace the values found in the PDF, fetched from the DOI or read from the added bibtex; the other fields are kept:

papers add paper.pdf --year 1999 --journal "Journal of Glaciology"
  • --key KEY sets the key, which is then not generated from the key template; without --key, the generated key uses the fields given (here the year 1999);
  • the files of --attach (and of a file field given with --metadata) are added to the files of the entry;
  • these options apply to one entry: they are an error with several files, a directory (-R), or a bibtex file of several entries;
  • an entry taken from a pool gets the fields given too (in the library; the pool entry changes only if you push);
  • when the added paper is already in the library (same DOI, see below), the fields of the library entry are not changed: papers warns that the options are ignored; use papers edit KEY to change them;
  • when the added entry is merged into a library entry by the duplicate check (below), the fields given are those of the added entry: a value that differs from the library's is a conflict, resolved as --on-duplicate says, and the library key is kept.

docs.title: Duplicates
docs.text: Before inserting an entry, papers add looks for the same paper in the library. papers check --duplicates and papers list --duplicates use the same rule (see Managing your library).

docs.title: Same paper
docs.text:
Two entries are the same paper when they have the same identifier, checked in this order:

  1. the DOI (case-insensitive; doi: and https://doi.org/ prefixes are ignored);
  2. the arXiv identifier: the eprint field when archivePrefix is arXiv or absent, and arXiv DOIs (10.48550/arXiv.<id>), whatever the version;
  3. the ISBN, for two @book entries only (a chapter carries the ISBN of its book, and each edition has its own ISBN);
  4. otherwise the family names of the authors and the title, compared without case, braces, accents and extra spaces. Both entries need authors and a title: two entries titled "Editorial" without authors are not the same paper. A name in braces is one name: and and commas inside braces ({Barnes and Noble}) do not separate names, as in BibTeX.

The first identifier that both entries have decides: equal values make the same paper, different values two papers. A preprint and the published article with different DOIs are two entries, even with the same authors and title.

Equal identifiers make the same paper, except in one case: when the entry types differ (e.g. @book and @incollection) and the titles differ (after ignoring case, braces, accents and spacing), papers asks instead of merging. This happens with a chapter exported with the DOI of its book, or a dataset "Data for: X" deposited under the DOI of the article "X". Without a terminal, such a pair is never merged.

When you answer that two entries are not the same paper (n, below), papers records it in .papers/distinct.json of the library, and does not ask about them again. The file records the identifiers of both entries (DOI, arXiv id, ISBN, authors and title), not their keys.

docs.title: What a merge does
docs.text:
The entry already in the library (entry 1) is the target:

  • it keeps its key;
  • fields that only the added entry has are added (except empty ones, such as pages = {});
  • the file links of both entries are kept (a file linked twice, or two copies with the same content, once);
  • values that differ only by case, braces, spaces, or the case of a DOI are not conflicts, and the library's spelling is kept. Author names with initials and with full first names (Smith, J. and Smith, John) are not a conflict either: the fuller form is kept, whichever entry it comes from. Different first names (Smith, John and Smith, Jane) are a conflict. First names are compared word by word up to the shorter one, so a missing middle name is not a conflict (Smith, J. and Smith, John Quincy);
  • the remaining differences are conflicts.

An added entry that brings nothing new (no conflict, no field to add) is merged without a question: its files are added, and papers prints already in library: smith2020climate (+1 file).

docs.title: --on-duplicate
docs.text:
--on-duplicate says what to do when the added entry has conflicts or fields to add:

Value What happens ask the dialogue below (default when the standard input is a terminal) keep merge; conflicts keep the library value update merge; conflicts take the value of the added entry skip the entry is not added; the library entry, its files and the added file are left as they are error stop before saving, and exit with status 1 (default without a terminal, e.g. in a script)

--no-check-duplicate adds the entries without looking for duplicates. An entry with the key of a library entry is still folded into it (its files added) when it is the same paper and the merge has nothing to decide (no conflict, no field to add); otherwise the command stops: pass -u/--update-key or --key KEY.

docs.title: The dialogue
docs.text:
$> papers add new.bib
Already in library: smith2020climate (same DOI 10.1000/abc123)
  1  library  smith2020climate  article  doi 10.1000/abc123  files/smith.pdf
  2  new      Smith_2020        article  doi 10.1000/ABC123  other/smith-preprint.pdf

@article{smith2020climate,
   author   = {Smith, John and Doe, Jane}
   doi      = {10.1000/abc123}
+  file     = {files/smith.pdf;other/smith-preprint.pdf}
!  journal  = {Nature}
!             2: {Nature Climate Change}
   keywords = {climate, mine}
   title    = {Climate sensitivity revisited}
+  volume   = {10}
   year     = {2020}
}
1 conflict. The key smith2020climate is kept; + lines are added.
  1 keep library values   2 take new values   f field by field   e edit
  n not the same paper (add Smith_2020 separately)   s skip   q quit   ? help
>>>

Unmarked lines are the same in both entries (here the title and the author names, which differ only by case and initials), + lines are added from the other entry, and ! lines are conflicts: the value that will be used, then the other values, numbered by entry.

Answer Meaning 1, 2 resolve all conflicts with the values of that entry, and merge f go through the conflicts one at a time e edit the merged entry in the editor, as plain bibtex; the values of the other entry are % comment lines below it. If the editor fails or the text is not one bibtex entry, papers comes back to this menu n not the same paper: add the entry separately (with a free key if its key is taken), and remember it s skip: change nothing for this entry; it is asked again next time q quit: skip this entry and all the remaining duplicates of this command; the other entries are added ? help

f asks for each conflict:

journal:
  1  Nature                 library
  2  Nature Climate Change  new
  [1/2/e] >>>

To stop without saving anything, use Ctrl-C.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
Entries added from a bibtex file keep their own key, unless -u/--update-key is passed, in which case the key is regenerated from the key template (see Renaming files and keys). Entries extracted from a PDF or fetched from a DOI always get a generated key. --key KEY sets the key instead, in both cases. Either way, this only concerns entries new to the library: an entry merged into a duplicate takes the key of the library entry.

A key that another entry has already (ignoring case) gets a letter suffix: Smith2000 becomes Smith2000b, then Smith2000c. A key that ends with a digit and a letter continues from that letter, in its case (Smith2000B gives Smith2000C); after z, a second letter is added (Smith2000za).

docs.title: Options of earlier versions
docs.text:
These options still work, with a warning, and will be removed:

Old New -m i --on-duplicate ask -m u --on-duplicate keep -m U --on-duplicate update (the library key is kept) -m o --on-duplicate update (the library key and the fields only in the library are kept) -m s --on-duplicate skip (the file of the added entry is not attached; keep does that) -m r --on-duplicate error -m a --no-check-duplicate --no-merge-files ignored: file links are always merged

docs.title: Libraries
docs.text:
A library is a bibtex file, a files directory, and a configuration file .papers/config.json in the library directory. The .papers/ folder also holds the origin copies of the entries exchanged with pools and the pairs recorded as not the same paper, also when the bibtex is in another folder. Versions up to 3.0.0b5 wrote these two next to the bibtex: papers moves them to the .papers/ of the library when it opens the library, unless the folder of the bibtex is a library of its own. papers init creates a library in the current directory, and papers init DIR in the directory DIR (created if missing, with its parents):

$> papers init
created the library ~/projects/sealevel
* bibtex:  papers.bib
* files:   files (the files directory of the library)
`papers config` lists and sets the settings

By default the library is self-contained (no pool), the bibtex is papers.bib (or the first .bib file present in the directory) and the files directory is files (or an existing pdfs, pdf, papers or bibliography folder). The options of papers init are --bibtex, --filesdir, --pool PATH and --shallow (see Pools), --global (see Global configuration), --paths relative|absolute, --editor and the name and key format options (see Renaming files and keys). With DIR, the paths given to --bibtex, --filesdir and --pool are relative to the current directory, as DIR is (papers init lib --bibtex lib/refs.bib). papers init does not prompt, and fails if the directory already has a library configuration: change the settings of an existing library with papers config.

Every command run in the library directory or in one of its subdirectories acts on that library. -C DIR, before the command name, runs papers as if it was started in DIR:

papers -C ~/projects/sealevel list smith

--bibtex and --filesdir still override the library for one command. If the bibtex given with --bibtex belongs to another library (a configuration file in its directory or above), the settings of that library apply.

Outside of any library, commands act on the default library if the global configuration sets one (see A global shared library), and otherwise fail: no library found here: papers init.

Type papers status to see which library a command acts on: where its bibtex and its files are, and how it stands with its pool. papers status -v also shows the number of steps of its history, the configuration file, the cache directory and the version. papers config lists the settings and where each one comes from.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
papers config gets and sets the settings, in the style of git config:

papers config                          # list the settings and where each comes from
papers config name.template            # print one setting
papers config name.template '{author}_{year}_{title}'   # set it in the library
papers config --unset name.template    # remove it from the library
papers config --prune                  # remove the values equal to the global or default value

Each setting comes from the library configuration if it sets it, otherwise from the global configuration, otherwise from its built-in default. The exception is pool: it comes only from the library configuration, and a library that does not set it has no pool (none). papers config without argument shows the source of each setting as (library), (global) or (default). In a shallow library, filesdir and the name.* settings are marked not used: shallow library: the files are in the pool, named with the pool's template (filesdir is where papers config pool none copies them).

The library configuration keeps the settings given to the library (papers init --paths absolute, papers config NAME VALUE), even when the value is the global or default one; the other settings follow the global configuration. papers config --unset NAME removes a setting from the file, and the library then follows the global configuration again. papers config --prune removes all the values equal to the global or default value (pool stays). Keys of the file that papers does not know (for example the settings of a newer version) are kept as they are when papers writes the file.

Setting Values bibtex path of the bibtex file filesdir path of the files directory pool path of the library's pool (relative to the library, or with ~): the library is shallow; or none (the value when the library does not set it): the library is self-contained (see Pools) paths relative (default) or absolute: how file links are written in the bibtex files move (default), copy, link or ask: what papers add, file attach and file rename do with a file outside the files directory (see Files); in a shallow library, how the file gets to the pool: moved or copied into its files directory, or linked where it is by the library and the pool entry auto-push false (default) or true: in a shallow library, the commands that change entries push them to the pool (the entries shared with it, and new ones), see Auto-push; no effect in a self-contained library checksums true (default): the commands write the checksum of the files they move, copy, add or link in .papers/files.json, for undo (see Checksums) editor command that opens a text editor, e.g. vim or subl -w (it wins over $VISUAL and $EDITOR, which are used without it) history-size 500 (default): the size of the history (see Undo and redo), in MB, 0 for no limit; papers asks before a command that deletes more. In the global configuration: the history shared by the libraries; in a library: its own history, with history-separate history-separate false (default) or true: the library keeps its history in a store of its own (see Where the history is) history-dir global only: the folder of the history (default: ~/.local/share/papers/history on Linux) keep-deleted-files global only: true (default) or false: the files that the commands delete are kept by the history, for undo; with false, they go to the trash of the system name.template, name.author-num, name.author-sep, name.title-word-num, name.title-word-size, name.title-length, name.title-sep, name.unknown-template, name.unknown-strict file name format key.template, key.author-num, key.author-sep, key.title-word-num, key.title-word-size, key.title-length, key.title-sep, key.unknown-template, key.unknown-strict bibtex key format

The name and key settings correspond to the --name-* and --key-* options of the commands (see Renaming files and keys), which override them for one command.

Paths in the library configuration are stored relative to its directory, so that the library can be moved or shared as a whole. papers config bibtex, papers config filesdir and the list of papers config show them as absolute paths.

A path given on the command line is relative to the current directory, as for any other command: papers config bibtex, papers config filesdir, papers config pool, papers config --global default and papers config --global history-dir, and papers init DIR --bibtex FILE --filesdir FOLDER --pool PATH (relative to the current directory, not to DIR). papers then stores it as the setting is written: relative to the library for bibtex and filesdir, as described below for pool, and absolute (with ~ for the home directory) for default and history-dir.

A configuration file (of a library or the global one) that is not valid JSON, or that gives a setting a value of the wrong type (for example "auto-push": "no" instead of false, or a number for pool), is an error: papers names the file and the setting and does nothing until the file is corrected.

history-dir and keep-deleted-files can only be set in the global configuration (papers config --global): a library you receive from someone cannot choose where your history goes, or what it keeps.

Setting paths rewrites the file links of the bibtex. Setting pool changes where the library links its files: pool PATH (an existing library without pool) links to the copies of the library's PDFs in PATH, and requires PATH to have them already (papers push --pool PATH copies them there); in a shallow library, pool none copies the pool files that the library links to into its files directory. papers lists what it will do and asks to continue (-y does not ask, --dry-run only lists; see Changing the pool).

docs.title: Global configuration
docs.text:
papers config --global reads and writes the global configuration (per user, as in git config --global) instead of the library's: ~/.config/papers/config.json on Linux (the platform's user configuration directory elsewhere). It holds the default settings of the libraries that do not set them (everything except bibtex, filesdir and pool: the global configuration has no pool), and optionally the default library.

papers config --global editor vim
papers config --global name.template '{author}_{year}'
papers config --global default ~/Documents/papers   # the default library
papers config --global                              # list it

default is the path of the default library, an existing library without pool, or none to remove it (--unset default too). It is used for two things: the library that commands act on outside of any library, and the pool of papers init --shallow. papers init PATH --global creates a self-contained library at PATH and sets it as the default library (papers init . --global for the current directory). papers migrate sets the global library of papers v2 as the default library. See A global shared library.

papers init stores pool and paths in the new library, taking their values from the global configuration when it sets them. The other settings are only stored in the library when you set them. Changing the default library later does not change the libraries created with papers init --shallow before: each keeps the pool written in its configuration.

docs.title: Pools
docs.text:
A pool is a library that other libraries exchange entries with (see Pools for add, pull, push and sync, and Export). A library has at most one pool, its pool setting: a path relative to the library (e.g. ../shared-with-bob), a path with ~ or absolute, or none. A library that does not set it has no pool. The pool must be an existing library without pool: papers init --pool PATH and papers config pool PATH check it, and stop otherwise. They also refuse a PATH that is the library itself (., or its path written another way). A pool that takes a pool of its own later is checked again by pull, push, sync and the commands that add entries or files to the pool: they stop with an error (the automatic push after a command prints a warning instead). papers init --shallow writes the default library of the global configuration as the pool, with ~ as the global configuration writes it, so that a project copied to another machine with the same layout finds its pool there.

A configuration file written by a test build that took several pools may store pool as a list: a list of one path is read as that path, and a list of several paths is an error that names the file. Write one path, or none, in that file.

The pool setting gives the state of the library. Without pool, the library is self-contained: its own entries and files. With a pool, it is shallow: its file links are the pool entry's, and the entries it adds go to the pool too; the library decides which entries it has. A project folder shared with others (git, Dropbox) should be self-contained: the links of a shallow library point into your own pool.

papers init                    # self-contained
papers init --pool ../shared   # shallow: the pool is ../shared
papers init --shallow          # shallow: the pool is the default library

papers status shows where the files of the library are: its files directory (self-contained library), or in the pool (shallow library). For a shallow library, it also shows the pool: its path, and how the library stands with it:

  • in sync: the entries exchanged with the pool are the same on both sides;
  • pool changed: the pool has changes to take, and the last line of papers status says how: `papers pull --dry-run` shows the changes, `papers pull` takes them;
  • library changed: the library has changes to send (papers push), e.g. made in an editor, or with auto-push off;
  • both changed: both (papers sync);
  • not pulled from yet: no entry was exchanged with the pool yet;
  • not pulled in full yet: entries were exchanged, but the pool was never pulled in full (only papers pull KEY, a pull that skipped a conflict, or a push that left the pool with something the library does not have), so papers does not know which pool changes the library has;
  • missing, not a library.

papers compares the entries, not only the files: a pool that changed in entries the library does not have, or the same change made on both sides, is in sync. It compares only the entries exchanged with the pool before (with an origin copy): an entry that the library and the pool both have but never exchanged is not compared; papers pull --dry-run finds those too. Once it found them in sync, papers remembers (with the history of the library, on the computer) the pieces of the library, of the pool and of the origin copies at that time, and later compares only the entries of the pieces that changed since: a single change does not cost a comparison of the whole library. papers status -v also shows the number of steps of the history of the library (see Undo and redo).

docs.title: Relative versus absolute paths
docs.text:
The file links in the bibtex are relative to the bibtex directory by default, so that a library folder can be moved or shared with its files. Set papers config paths absolute to store absolute paths instead, e.g. for a bibtex that links to files in a central folder.

papers rewrites the links to the setting when it reads the bibtex: with absolute, all links; with relative, the absolute links (for example written by another program). The bibtex is written with them at the next command that saves it. On Windows, a link to a file on another drive than the bibtex stays absolute.

The options --relative-paths and --absolute-paths of the commands still override the setting for one command, with a deprecation warning.

A library in the git repository of a project leaves .papers/ out of it (papers writes .papers/.gitignore): see Using git.

docs.title: Migrating from papers 2
docs.text:
Upgrading from papers 2 gives an overview. papers migrate performs the one-time upgrades from version 2:

  • The global configuration of version 2 (~/.config/papersconfig.json on Linux) defined a library for the whole user account. papers migrate writes its settings to a library configuration .papers/config.json in the directory of its bibtex (if there is none yet; a self-contained library: it keeps its files and has no pool), registers the directory of that bibtex as the default library in the global configuration (unless another default library is set there), and renames the old file to papersconfig.json.v2.bak. The bibtex and files stay where they are. File links stay absolute, as they were, unless --relative is passed. Running papers migrate again does nothing. Until then, papers prints a warning and keeps using the global configuration outside of libraries.
  • papers migrate --folders moves the files of entries that are still kept in folders of papers before 2.19 (<name>/ with a hidden .<name>.bib) into the files directory, named after the name template (as papers file rename names them).

Library configurations of version 2 keep working without migration: they are read as self-contained libraries (their files are their own, no pool), as in version 2. Their file is moved to .papers/config.json the next time papers writes the configuration (e.g. papers config, or the first command that changes the library, which adds the id of its history), or by papers migrate run in the library (see Upgrading from papers 2). The configuration files written by version 3 carry "version": 3; a file without version is read as a file of version 2. A file with a higher version was written by a newer papers, and papers stops with an error.

docs.title: papers install
docs.text: papers install is a deprecated alias of papers init that asks for the bibtex and the files directory (-y/--yes accepts the defaults; --no-prompt and --force are its deprecated forms). On an existing library it updates the library configuration, as in version 2, with a deprecation warning: use papers config instead (--edit and --reset keep working). papers install --global is no longer supported: it stops with an error and changes nothing. Create the default library with papers init PATH --global (for example papers init ~/Documents/papers/default --global), or register an existing library with papers config --global default PATH. --local is ignored.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
papers uninstall is deprecated: rm -r .papers removes the configuration of a library, and papers history --remove its history. papers uninstall removes the library configuration and reports what it leaves behind (the bibtex file, the files directory, the history). --remove-history (or its older name --remove-backup) also removes the history. It never removes the global configuration. From outside of any library it does not remove the default library's configuration: run papers -C DIR uninstall for that.

papers uninstall --recursive is deprecated and ignored (there is no global library configuration to walk up to in v3): only the configuration of the library is removed.

docs.title: Cache
docs.text: All internet requests, such as crossref requests, are saved in the cache directory (shown by papers status -v), whether or not a library is configured. The metadata of each DOI is a json file under doi/, e.g. doi/10.1126/science.1166510.json (DOIs that do not exist are remembered for a day), the searches of --openalex are under openalex/, and the open-access locations of a DOI (papers file fetch) under openalex-work/ (asked again after 30 days: a paper can become open access). downloads/ has, for each URL of a PDF that papers file fetch (or add --fetch-pdf, fetch --pdf) downloaded, the checksum (sha256) and size of the file it gave: a URL whose file the entry or the library already has is not downloaded again. Deleting the directory, or any file in it, is safe: the requests are made again when needed.

docs.title: papers export
docs.text:
papers export DIR [KEY...|-] [--files copy|link|none] [--format FORMAT]

writes the entries (all without KEY) as a new library in DIR, which must not exist or be empty, to hand over: its bibtex, its files directory, and its configuration (a self-contained library, with the name and key templates that the library sets). File links are relative to the new bibtex. --format writes RIS, CSL-JSON or BibJSON as well, or instead (see Other formats).

  • --files copy (default) copies the files into DIR/files (hard links when possible), named with the name template;
  • --files link links to the files where they are;
  • --files none leaves the file links out.
$ papers export ~/export-test perrette_landerer2013
create the library ~/export-test
exported 1 entries to ~/export-test (papers.bib; files: copy)
$ ls ~/export-test ~/export-test/files
~/export-test:
files
papers.bib

~/export-test/files:
perrette_et_al_2013_a-scaling-approach-to-project-regional-sea-level-rise-and-its-uncertainties.pdf

papers add DIR --recursive adds an exported library to another one (its bibtex and PDFs; the RIS and JSON files of a folder are left out: add one with papers add DIR/papers.ris), and papers config pool DIR makes it the pool of the library (the export has copies of its PDFs). papers sync --pool DIR exchanges entries with it later (see Exchanges with any library).

docs.title: Other formats: RIS, CSL-JSON and BibJSON
docs.text:
papers export DIR [KEY...|-] --format bib|ris|csl-json|bibjson|all

--format chooses the files of entries written in DIR, next to DIR/files:

format file bib (default) papers.bib bibtex; DIR is a papers library, as above ris papers.ris RIS, read by Zotero, EndNote, Mendeley...; needs the rispy package (see Installation) csl-json papers.json CSL-JSON, read by Zotero, pandoc and citeproc processors bibjson (or bib.json) papers.bib.json BibJSON: the bibtex fields as they are, in JSON, for programs (see BibJSON) all the four files

The files are written in UTF-8 with \n line ends on every platform, as the bibtex.

Repeat the option or separate the formats with commas (--format bib,ris). The file links of each file point to the copies in DIR/files, relative to DIR (with --files link, to the files where they are). Without bib, DIR is not a papers library (it has no .papers/config.json and no bibtex, which would be named as the bibtex of the library), and papers says so:

$ papers export ~/export-test --format all
create the library ~/export-test
exported 1 entries to ~/export-test (papers.bib, papers.ris, papers.json, papers.bib.json; files: copy)
$ papers export ~/for-zotero --format ris
exported 1 entries to ~/for-zotero (papers.ris; files: copy)
~/for-zotero is not a papers library (no papers.bib): --format bib or all makes one
$ cat ~/for-zotero/papers.ris
TY  - JOUR
ID  - perrette_landerer2013
AU  - Perrette, M.
AU  - Landerer, F.
AU  - Riva, R.
AU  - Frieler, K.
AU  - Meinshausen, M.
TI  - A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and its uncertainties
T2  - Earth System Dynamics
PY  - 2013
VL  - 4
IS  - 1
SP  - 11
EP  - 29
DO  - 10.5194/esd-4-11-2013
L1  - files/perrette_et_al_2013_a-scaling-approach-to-project-regional-sea-level-rise-and-its-uncertainties.pdf
ER  -

papers list --format ris, --format csl-json and --format bibjson write the entries to the standard output instead, without copying files (see Output formats). papers add refs.ris, papers add refs.json and papers add refs.bib.json read these formats (see Add RIS, CSL-JSON and BibJSON files).

docs.title: How the fields are converted
docs.text:
The values are written as unicode (LaTeX accents and commands are converted, braces removed). Fields without an equivalent in the format are left out.

The conversion from LaTeX to unicode is that of the pylatexenc library (through bibtexparser), also used by papers check --encoding unicode and for the entry fetched for an added PDF or DOI. Its exact text can change with the version of the library; papers does not read it back nor compare it.

bibtex CSL-JSON RIS key id, citation-key ID entry type type (below) TY (below) author, editor, translator author, editor, translator (family, given, non-dropping-particle, suffix; a name in braces is a literal) AU, ED, A4 (Family, Given, Suffix) title title TI journal, booktitle container-title T2 series collection-title T3 year, month issued (date-parts) PY, DA volume volume VL number, issue issue (articles), else number IS pages page (11-29) SP, EP doi, url DOI, URL DO, UR urldate accessed Y2 isbn, issn ISBN, ISSN SN publisher (or school, institution) publisher PB address publisher-place CY abstract, keywords, note abstract, keyword, note AB, KW, N1 edition, language edition, language ET, LA file custom.file (a list) L1 (one line per file)

CSL-JSON has no field for files: the links are written in its custom object, "custom": {"file": [...]}, which other programs ignore.

A mastersthesis is a thesis of genre Master's thesis in CSL-JSON, and a THES record with M3 - Master's thesis in RIS (unless the entry has a type field), so that it is read back as a mastersthesis.

bibtex CSL-JSON RIS article article-journal JOUR book book BOOK inbook, incollection chapter CHAP inproceedings, conference paper-conference CPAPER proceedings book CONF phdthesis, mastersthesis thesis THES techreport report RPRT misc document GEN online webpage ELEC dataset, software dataset, software DATA, COMP unpublished manuscript UNPB

docs.title: BibJSON
docs.text:
BibJSON is the convention of the Open Knowledge Foundation for bibliographic records in JSON. RIS and CSL-JSON convert the fields to those of other programs and lose some of them; BibJSON keeps the bibtex fields as they are (LaTeX included), so that a program can read the whole library:

$ papers list perrette --format bibjson
{
  "metadata": {
    "records": 1
  },
  "records": [
    {
      "type": "article",
      "id": "perrette_landerer2013",
      "author": [
        {
          "name": "Perrette, M."
        },
        ...
      ],
      "journal": {
        "name": "Earth System Dynamics"
      },
      "title": "A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and its uncertainties",
      "year": "2013",
      "file": [
        "/home/me/papers/files/perrette_et_al_2013_a-scaling-approach-to-project-regional-sea-level-rise-and-its-uncertainties.pdf"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
  • type and id are the entry type and key;
  • author and editor are lists of {"name": ...}, and journal is {"name": ...}, as BibJSON gives them;
  • the other fields are strings, as in the bibtex;
  • file is the list of the file links (absolute paths with papers list, relative to DIR with papers export);
  • a bibtex field with the name of a BibJSON key (type, id, cid, collection, identifier, link, license), e.g. the type of a techreport (type = {Working paper}), is written as bibtex:type, and the collection's metadata declares the namespace ("namespace": {"bibtex": ...}), as BibJSON says for additional keys. papers reads it back as the bibtex field.

papers add refs.bib.json reads a collection ({"records": [...]}), a list of records or one record. It also reads the DOI of BibJSON identifiers ("identifier": [{"type": "doi", "id": ...}]), and joins the lists of strings (e.g. keywords) with commas, leaving out null items. Numbers are kept as written in the file (0.0000001, 2000.0).

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
An entry links to its files (the PDF, supplementary material...) in its file field. The files usually live in the files directory of the library (the filesdir setting), named after the name template (see Renaming files and keys), but an entry can link to a file anywhere.

The file field holds the links separated by ;. Each link is path, path:type or description:path:type; papers writes :path:type (:files/x.pdf:pdf), as JabRef and Zotero do. In the three-part form, the path is everything between the first and the last :, so it may contain : (:C:\x.pdf:pdf). Spaces around each path are removed. There is no escaping: a path that contains ; cannot be linked, JabRef's \: and \; are read as they are, and a Windows path written alone (C:\x.pdf) is read as the path C with type \x.pdf.

docs.title: What add does with a file
docs.text:
The files setting says what papers add does with the PDF it adds, with the files of the entries of an added bibtex (papers add other.bib), with the files of an added folder (papers add --recursive DIR) and with the files attached with --attach:

files the file is placed in the files directory the original is removed move (default) yes, under its template name yes ask papers asks for each file: move, copy or leave it (link) as answered copy yes, as a hard link when possible (same file system), otherwise a copy no link no: the entry links to the file where it is no

With ask, papers names each file that is outside the files directory and waits for an answer: m (move), c (copy) or l (leave it where it is, also Enter); M, C or L gives the same answer for all the next files of the command. A file already in the files directory is renamed without asking. Without a terminal (a script, a pipe), papers does not ask: the files are left where they are, with a warning.

Set it for a library with papers config files copy, or for all libraries of the user with papers config --global files copy. The options --move, --copy and --link of papers add override it for one command; -r/--rename is the same as --move, and -c the same as --copy. papers file attach, papers file rename (--keep-source is the same as --copy) and papers list --rename (with --move or --keep-source) follow the setting too.

A file that belongs to another library, i.e. a file inside the files directory of a library whose configuration (.papers/config.json) is found in the file's directory or above, is never moved: in move mode it is copied instead (a hard link when possible), so that the other library keeps its link. The same holds for a file in the files directory of the pool of the library, or of the library of --pool PATH (see Pools). A file already in the files directory of the current library is renamed in copy mode too, rather than copied next to itself. A file downloaded by papers (a URL given to add or --attach) is always moved into the files directory.

In a shallow library (a library with a pool), the file links are the pool entry's; the library decides which entries it has. The files directory where add, file attach and file rename place the files is that of the pool, and the name template is the pool's: move and copy place the file in the pool's files directory, and the library entry and the pool entry link to it there; with link, the file stays where it is, and both link to it there. This works on one machine; on another machine that uses the pool, such links are broken (see Shallow libraries).

docs.title: papers file
docs.text:
The commands of papers file act on the files of the entries. Those that take entries accept keys, DOIs, arXiv identifiers or ISBNs (see Naming entries), and - to read them from the standard input, one per line:

Command Action papers file rename [KEY...] place the files of the entries (all without KEY) in the files directory, under their template name; --keep-source keeps the originals too (hard links when possible) papers file mv SRC... DEST move files or folders, and update the links of the entries (below) papers file attach KEY FILE... attach files to an existing entry, following the files setting (--move, --copy, --link override it); the files the entry already has are not touched papers file fetch KEY..., papers file fetch --missing download the free PDF of the entries (from their DOI or arXiv id) and attach it (below) papers file fetch --upgrade [KEY...] replace an accepted manuscript or a submitted version by the published version, when it can be had (below) papers file detach FILE... [--key KEY...] remove the links to the files from every entry that links to them (only from the entries of --key with --key); the files are kept (below) papers file detach --key KEY... remove all the links of the entries papers file detach --broken [--key KEY...] remove the broken links (of all entries without --key) papers file rm FILE... [-r] [--key KEY...] remove the links to the files, then delete the files, like git rm (below) papers file check [KEY...] report broken links and the files found for them (in the library by checksum, in the pool, in the libraries of --pool PATH, in the other libraries of the machine, and in the folders of --search DIR), files linked twice, identical files (same checksum) of an entry, and with --metadata a DOI of the PDF that differs from the DOI of the entry (this parses the PDFs) papers file fix [KEY...] apply the repairs that papers file check reports (below); --pool PATH and --search DIR as for check; the files found are copied, never moved (--move moves those of --search) papers file clean remove the files of the files directory and its subfolders that no entry links to, asking for each one (-y/--yes does not ask)

papers file attach KEY FILE... is the low-level form of papers add FILE --doi DOI for an entry already in the library: when the DOI is that of a library entry, add attaches the file to it in the same way, without fetching anything (see Adding entries).

papers file check changes nothing, and ends with the number of links that papers file fix can repair. papers file fix only applies the repairs that cannot lose anything: paths saved by Mendeley (missing leading /, latex symbols such as {\_}) are repaired when the repaired path exists, the second link to the same file, or to an identical file, is removed from the entry (the file itself stays on disk; papers file clean removes it), and broken links are relinked to the files found for them (see Reconnecting PDFs and a bibtex). The other broken links are reported, and removed with papers file detach --broken.

papers file clean skips hidden files and folders (such as .git) and .bib files. A folder of the layout of versions before 2.19 (with a hidden .<name>.bib) is removed as a whole when no entry links to its files.

docs.title: Fetching the free PDF of an entry
docs.text:
papers file fetch KEY... finds an open-access PDF of each entry from its DOI or arXiv id, downloads it, and attaches it as papers file attach does: the PDF goes to the files directory, under the template name of the entry. --missing takes the entries without PDF (of the KEYs given, or of the whole library). Only open-access copies are used. The links are tried in this order, until one gives a PDF (a file that starts with %PDF; a login page or a challenge is not one):

  1. the published version: the PDF that the publisher's article page links (its citation_pdf_url tag, the page being that of https://doi.org/DOI), then the open-access locations of OpenAlex of the published version: their PDF links, then the PDF that the landing pages of the others give in their citation_pdf_url tag (repositories such as DSpace, Pure or PubMan);
  2. the accepted manuscript (OpenAlex, in the same way);
  3. the submitted version (OpenAlex, in the same way), then arXiv (https://arxiv.org/pdf/ID).

Each line says which version was attached and where it came from:

$ papers file fetch smith2020 doe2021
smith2020: files/smith_2020_ocean.pdf (published version, from journals.example.org)
doe2021: files/doe_2021_ice.pdf (accepted manuscript, from repository.example.edu)

When the published version was refused (an HTTP error, or a login page or a challenge instead of a PDF) and an accepted manuscript or a submitted version is attached instead, the line also gives the published link, to download it in a browser:

doe2021: files/doe_2021_ice.pdf (accepted manuscript, from repository.example.edu; the published version was refused: open https://journals.example.org/ice.pdf in a browser)

--version published attaches the published version only, --version accepted also the accepted manuscript. When no link gives a PDF, the error lists the links tried and the pages to open in a browser; the other entries are attached and saved, and the command exits with status 1. In a fetch of several entries, an entry without PDF is one line (KEY: no PDF (...), with the same reasons and links), not an error:

lee2019: no PDF (https://journals.example.org/sea.pdf (published version): not a PDF; OpenAlex: no open-access PDF; open https://journals.example.org/sea.pdf, https://doi.org/10.1000/sea in a browser)
``` `--dry-run`
lists the links that would be tried, in order, and changes nothing.

A fetch of several entries (`--missing`, or several KEYs) ends with a
summary: the PDFs attached by version, the entries repaired from a local
file, and the links to open in a browser for the entries without PDF and
those whose published version was refused:
summary of 4 entries: 2 PDFs attached: 1 published version, 1 accepted manuscript 1 found locally (repaired, not downloaded) 1 without PDF open in a browser: doe2021: https://journals.example.org/ice.pdf (published version refused; accepted manuscript found) lee2019: https://journals.example.org/sea.pdf, https://doi.org/10.1000/sea (no PDF) 
`--supplements` also attaches the supplementary PDFs that the article page
links: the links to a PDF with `suppl` in their URL or their text, and the
`citation_supplementary_material` tags. They are attached as the other files
of the entry (`<name>--<label>.pdf`). Data sets and other files are left
out; what is found depends on the publisher.

Nothing is downloaded or attached twice:

- an entry that links to a PDF already is skipped (`KEY: has a PDF already
  (--again to fetch it anyway)`); with `--supplements`, its supplements are
  still fetched;
- an entry whose PDF link is broken first gets the repair of
  `papers file fix` (see [Reconnecting PDFs and a bibtex](#reconnecting-pdfs-and-a-bibtex)):
  the file found in the library by checksum, in the pool, in the other
  libraries of the machine, in the folders of `--search DIR` (the option
  can be repeated) or in the history is relinked, and nothing is downloaded
  (`KEY: relinked files/x.pdf (found in ~/Downloads), not downloaded`). The
  PDF is downloaded only when no file is found. `--dry-run` says what would
  be relinked. The repair and the downloads are one step: `papers undo`
  undoes both;
- a downloaded file with the content (sha256) of a file of the entry is not
  attached (`not attached, the entry has the same file`);
- papers remembers, in the cache of the machine (see
  [Configuration](configuration.md#cache)), the checksum of the PDF each URL
  gave. A URL downloaded before is not downloaded again when the entry has a
  file with that checksum (`KEY: already has FILE`), or when a file of the
  library has it: that file is attached instead (a file of another entry is
  linked where it is, `same file as OTHERKEY`). Nothing about the URL is
  written in the library (only the version of the PDF, below).

With `--missing`, when more than 50 entries with a DOI would query OpenAlex
and no API key is set (environment variable `OPENALEX_API_KEY`, free at
<https://openalex.org/settings/api>), papers asks first (`-y/--yes` does not
ask; without a terminal, it stops and says how to proceed). The email
address of `PAPERS_MAILTO`, when set, is given to OpenAlex and in the user
agent of the requests to the publishers. papers waits a second between two
requests to the same site; a site that answers "too many requests" (HTTP
429) is asked once more after the wait it gives (at most 30 seconds).

The version of each PDF attached this way is kept in the library
(`.papers/files.json`, by the checksum of the file): it follows the file when
it is renamed or moved, and `papers list` shows it (see
[Listing](listing.md#output-formats)). A file attached otherwise (`papers file
attach`, `papers add FILE`) has no version: it is unknown.

`papers file fetch --upgrade` looks again for the published version of the
entries whose PDF is an accepted manuscript or a submitted version (all such
entries, or those of KEY...), and only for it. When it is found, it replaces
that PDF under the same file name; the old file is kept in the history, so
`papers undo` brings it back. When it is not found, nothing changes:
$ papers file fetch --upgrade doe2021: files/doe_2021_ice.pdf: accepted manuscript replaced by the published version, from journals.example.org lee2019: files/lee_2019_sea.pdf (submitted version) kept (no published version: https://journals.example.org/sea.pdf (published version): HTTP 403; open https://journals.example.org/sea.pdf, https://doi.org/10.1000/sea in a browser) summary of 2 entries: 1 replaced by the published version 1 without published version (kept as they are) open in a browser: lee2019: https://journals.example.org/sea.pdf, https://doi.org/10.1000/sea (no published version) 
`--dry-run` lists the links that would be tried and the file each would
replace. `--upgrade` does not go with `--missing`, `--again`,
`--supplements`, `--version` or `--search`.

`papers add --doi DOI --fetch-pdf` adds the entry and fetches its PDF in the
same way, and `papers fetch --pdf DOI` downloads the PDF into the current
directory (`-o FILE` names the file), without a library (see
[Adding entries](adding-entries.md#add-an-entry-from-its-doi)).

### Moving files

`papers file mv` works like `mv`, with the rules of `git mv`, and updates the
links of every entry that links to a moved file (links are compared by real
path, so a link through a symbolic link is found too):

1. a source file that no entry links to is an error;
2. a source folder must contain at least one linked file; the whole folder
   moves, files that no entry links to included;
3. with several sources, the destination must be an existing folder;
4. a destination that exists as a file is an error, unless `-f/--force`
   (papers warns when entries link to the replaced file: their links then
   lead to the moved file);
5. `-n/--dry-run` shows the moves and the links that change, and does
   nothing;
6. moving the files directory of the library (or a folder that contains it)
   also updates the `filesdir` setting.

All checks run before anything moves: if one fails, nothing is moved. If a
move fails midway (e.g. disk full), the bibtex is saved with the links of the
files already moved, and the error is reported. The parent folders of the
destination are created when needed. A folder that contains the bibtex or
the library configuration cannot be moved with `papers file mv`.
papers file mv files/2013 files/archive/2013 papers file mv files ~/Documents/library-files # also sets filesdir papers file mv -n files/a.pdf files/b.pdf files/new/ 
Links from other libraries to the moved files break: papers cannot know
about them.

### Detaching and removing files

A file can be linked from several entries: the chapters of a book that
share the PDF of the volume, two papers that share a supplement.
`papers file detach FILE...` removes the links to FILE from all of them and
prints which entries lost a link. Links are compared by real path, so a
broken link can be named too. The files stay on disk: `papers file detach`
never deletes a file.

`papers file rm FILE...` works like `git rm`: it removes the links to FILE
from every entry that links to it, then deletes the file.

- A FILE that no entry links to is an error, and nothing changes (with
  `--key`: that none of the entries of `--key` links to).
- `-r FOLDER` removes the linked files inside FOLDER (and its subfolders).
  Files that no entry links to stay where they are; the folders left empty
  are removed, FOLDER included, except the files directory of the library.
  Without `-r`, a folder is an error. `papers file detach -r FOLDER` removes
  the links in the same way, without deleting anything.
- With `--key`, only the links of those entries are removed; a file that
  another entry still links to is kept on disk, and papers says so.
- In a shallow library, the link is removed from the pool entry too, and
  the file (in the pool's files directory or elsewhere) is deleted unless
  another entry of the pool or of the library still links to it.
- papers does not ask: the file was named on the command line. `--dry-run`
  shows the links that would be removed and the files and folders that
  would be deleted.

`-k/--key` takes one or more entries (keys, DOIs, arXiv identifiers or
ISBNs), and can be repeated: `--key K1 K2` is `--key K1 --key K2`; `-`
reads them from the standard input. As it takes several values, write the
files before it: in `papers file rm --key K1 file.pdf`, `file.pdf` would be
read as an entry, and papers stops with the error `file.pdf is not an
entry: put the files before --key`.
papers file detach files/volume.pdf # from all the chapters papers file detach files/volume.pdf --key smith2020 # from one chapter papers file detach --key smith2020 # all its links papers file rm files/old-version.pdf papers file rm -r files/2013 --dry-run papers list --tag draft --detach-broken 
## Reconnecting PDFs and a bibtex

When the links of a library are broken because the PDFs moved (another
library that shared the files directory moved them into a library, a folder
was renamed, a backup was restored elsewhere...), `papers file fix`
looks for each missing file, without parsing any PDF:

1. in the library itself, by checksum: when `.papers/files.json` has the
   checksum of the missing file (see `papers file checksum`), a file of the
   library with that content: a file of another entry (linked where it is,
   `same content as the file of KEY`), or a file of the files directory
   that no entry links to (renamed by hand, for example; it is placed under
   the template name);
2. in the pool of the library, among the files of the pool entry of the
   same paper (same DOI, arXiv identifier, ISBN, or same title and
   authors): the file with the same file name as the broken link; else
   the one file named `<name>--<file name of the link>` (the pool renamed
   it as an attachment, see
   [Renaming files and keys](renaming.md#entries-with-several-files));
   then, if one broken link of the entry and one file of the pool entry
   are left, that file. When more are left, nothing is guessed. Then by
   checksum, among the files of the pool's `.papers/files.json`;
3. in the libraries given with `--pool PATH` (the option can be repeated),
   in the same way: the entry of PATH of the same paper, and its files.
   PATH must be a library (otherwise: `create it first with papers init`).
   Nothing changes in PATH, and no origin copy is recorded (see
   [Origin copies](pools.md#origin-copies)): only the file links of the
   library change;
4. in the other libraries of the machine, by checksum: those that the
   history knows (`papers history --all` lists them), except the library
   and its pool. A file with the checksum that `.papers/files.json` has for
   the missing file, among the files of their `.papers/files.json` as of
   their last papers command (a change made there by hand is seen after
   the next papers command in that library). A library that moved or was
   deleted is skipped, and nothing is written in the other libraries
   (`found in ~/other/library`);
5. in the folders given with `--search DIR` (searched recursively; the
   option can be repeated): a file with the same file name as the broken
   link, else a file named as the library's name template names the entry
   (with the extension of the link). When several files match, none is
   taken, and papers says which;
6. in the history (see [Undo and redo](undo-redo.md#deleted-files)): a file
   that a papers command deleted from the place of the link (or whose
   checksum `.papers/files.json` has, if the history keeps a file with that
   content) is copied back there, and the link stays as it is
   (`one2000: files/a.pdf: restored from the history (deleted by step
   4f1c9a2e)`). `papers undo` removes it again. The step of `papers file
   fix` keeps the file in the history too, so that undo and redo still
   work once the step that deleted it is dropped.

The file found in the pool, `--pool PATH`, another library or a `--search`
folder replaces the broken link. It is never moved, whatever the
`files` setting:

- in a self-contained library, it is copied (a hard link when possible)
  into the files directory, named as `papers file attach KEY FILE` names
  it;
- in a shallow library, a file of its pool is linked where it is; a file of
  `--pool PATH`, of another library or of a `--search` folder is copied into the files
  directory of the pool, and the pool entry links to it (as for the other
  changes of file links, see
  [Shallow libraries](shallow-libraries.md#files));
- in `link` mode, or in a library without files directory, the file is
  linked where it is.

`papers file fix --move` moves the files found in the `--search` folders
instead of copying them. A file in the files directory of another library
is still copied (`... belongs to the library in ...: copied, not moved`),
and so are the files of the pool, of `--pool PATH` and of the other
libraries.

`papers config pool PATH` links the library to the copies in PATH of the
files that exist, and says how many links were already broken:
`papers file fix` relinks them afterwards.

`papers file check` takes `--pool PATH` and `--search DIR` too, reports the
files that `papers file fix` would relink and where they come from, and
ends with the `papers file fix` command to run, with the same `-C DIR`,
`--bibtex FILE`, KEYs, `--pool` and `--search`. `papers file fix --dry-run`
shows the links that it would change, and changes nothing. After
`papers file fix`, the last line counts the issues left, if any.
$ papers file check --pool ~/P --search ~/Downloads perrette2013scaling: broken link: ~/old/esd-4-11-2013.pdf -> ~/P/files/perrette_2013_a-scaling-approach.pdf (from the library ~/P) perrette2011: broken link: ~/old/bg-8-515-2011.pdf -> ~/Downloads/bg-8-515-2011.pdf (found in ~/Downloads) 2 links can be relinked, 0 without a file found 2 issue(s) in the files of 2 entries 2 links can be repaired: papers file fix --pool ~/P --search ~/Downloads $ papers file fix --pool ~/P --search ~/Downloads perrette2013scaling: relinked to ~/thesis/files/perrette_2013_a-scaling-approach-to-project-regional-sea-level-rise.pdf (from the library ~/P) perrette2011: relinked to ~/thesis/files/perrette_2011_near-ubiquity-of-ice-edge-blooms-in-the-arctic.pdf (found in ~/Downloads) 2 links relinked, 0 still broken 
`papers file fix` works on any bibtex, without `papers init`: there is no
files directory, and the files found are linked where they are.
$ papers file fix --bibtex refs.bib --search ~/Downloads perrette2011: relinked to ~/Downloads/bg-8-515-2011.pdf (found in ~/Downloads) 1 link relinked, 0 still broken ```

For PDFs whose names say nothing about the paper, papers add -R DIR is the fallback: it parses each PDF, and a PDF with the DOI of a library entry is attached to that entry, without new entry and without duplicate dialogue (a PDF with the content of a file of the entry is not attached again; see Adding entries). The broken links stay next to the new ones: remove them with papers file detach --broken.

docs.title: Removing entries and their files
docs.text:
papers rm KEY... (or papers list ... --delete) removes entries. Their files that no remaining entry links to may be deleted too:

  • in a terminal, papers lists those that are inside the files directory and asks once whether to delete them (default: no);
  • --delete-files deletes them without asking, and also those outside the files directory; --keep-files keeps them without asking;
  • without a terminal (e.g. the keys come from a pipe), the files are kept, and papers lists them: papers file clean deletes them later;
  • a file outside the files directory is deleted only with --delete-files.

A file still linked from another entry is never deleted, nor a file in the files directory of the pool of the library, nor, in a shallow library, a file that an entry of the pool links to (see Shallow libraries); papers rm does not change the pool. In a shallow library, --delete-files is an error and nothing is removed: the files are the pool's, and papers file rm FILE deletes them. A file that is a hard link (e.g. to the file of another library) can be deleted: this only removes this link, and papers says so.

docs.title: Deprecated forms
docs.text: papers filecheck still works in v3, with a warning, and runs the corresponding commands: --rename (-c) is papers file rename (--keep-source), --delete-broken is papers file detach --broken, --hash-check and --fix-mendeley are papers file fix, --metadata-check is papers file check --metadata, and --clean-filesdir (--force) is papers file clean (--yes). papers list --copy and --add-files are deprecated too (now --rename --keep-source and --attach, see Listing and searching), and so is papers add --attachment (now --attach; -a FILE attaches the file until v4, with a warning: -a is --author, see Adding entries).

docs.title: Using git
docs.text:
papers does not use git: it keeps its own history of each library for undo and redo (see Undo and redo), on your computer, outside the library. That history is a way to repair mistakes, not a record of your work: it is not synced, and it keeps a limited size.

If you want the history of your bibliography and PDFs, or to share them, put the library folder under git yourself, like any other project:

cd ~/projects/sealevel
git init
git add papers.bib files .papers
git commit -m "my library"

papers never commits to that repository, and leaves it alone.

docs.title: The folder .papers/
docs.text:
The bibtex and the PDFs are your work. The folder .papers/ holds the internals of papers: what it keeps to manage them, which may change from one version to the next. papers writes .papers/.gitignore (with *), so that git leaves the folder out. A colleague who clones the repository runs papers init to make it a library on their side.

As git does with its own .git/config, each copy of a library has its own settings. To commit the configuration nonetheless (so that a clone is a library right away), make .papers/.gitignore:

*
!.gitignore
!config.json

papers does not rewrite a .gitignore you changed. What is in the folder:

file what it is without it config.json the settings of the library: where its bibtex and files are, its pool, the name formats, its identifier set them again (papers init, papers config) origin/ with a pool only: each entry as it was at the last pull or push, to tell who changed what since the next pull asks about more differences distinct.json the pairs of entries you said are not the same paper papers asks about them again files.json the checksums of the files, for undo nothing: papers file checksum writes them again

docs.title: Backups of earlier versions
docs.text:
Earlier versions of papers kept a git backup of each library: in the library, .papers/backup (the v3 branch before 3.0.0b4), or in a folder of the computer, ~/.local/share/papers/backups (papers 3.0.0b2 and earlier). papers no longer uses them, and does not delete them: papers history lists those it finds, with their size, and the command that deletes them:

stale: ~/projects/sealevel/.papers/backup (backup of an earlier papers, 641 MB, no longer used) — delete with: rm -rf ~/projects/sealevel/.papers/backup

Their history does not carry over: undo starts with the first command made with this version. The settings git and git-lfs, papers init --git, --git-lfs and papers git are no longer used.

docs.title: A global shared library
docs.text:
One way to use papers: a single library, for instance ~/Documents/papers, holds all your entries and PDFs, and each project is a shallow library that uses it as pool. A paper is fetched and stored once, the first time a project adds it; the other projects take it from the shared library. This is close to the global library of papers 2, with one bibtex per project on top.

papers supports this with an optional default library in the global configuration (~/.config/papers/config.json on Linux):

  • papers init --shallow creates a shallow library whose pool is the default library;
