Coming from papers 2: see Upgrading from papers 2.

docs.title: Entries with several files
docs.text:
The first file of an entry (the PDF) is named after the name template, and any other file (attachments, e.g. supplementary material added with --attach or papers file attach) is placed next to it, under the same name followed by -- and the file's original name:

files/perrette_et_al_2013_a-scaling-approach.pdf
files/perrette_et_al_2013_a-scaling-approach--esd-4-11-2013-supplement.pdf

The label after -- is kept when the entry is renamed again (e.g. after its title or year was fixed), so only the part before -- changes. If two attachments have the same original name, the second one gets a -2 suffix.

Two entries can get the same file name (the same authors, year and title, e.g. a preprint and the published paper). A file of another entry is never replaced: the second file gets a -2 suffix (-3, ... after that), unless it has the same content, in which case both entries link to the same file.

Versions before 2.19 placed the files of an entry with several files in a folder named after the entry, with a hidden copy of the entry (files/<name>/.<name>.bib). Such folders keep working as they are: their files are linked from the bibtex, and nothing is moved until the entry is renamed. Renaming (papers file rename) moves the files out of the folder into the layout above, and removes the folder if nothing but the hidden bibtex is left in it (a folder with other files is kept, and the files left in it are reported).

docs.title: Renaming the files of existing entries
docs.text:
papers add places new files in the files directory under their template name (unless the files setting is link, see Files). To rename the files of entries already in the library, e.g. after changing the name template or fixing an entry's title:

papers file rename                      # all entries
papers file rename perrette2013         # some entries
papers list --year 2013 --rename       # the listed entries

A file already in the files directory is renamed. A file outside it (e.g. in a folder of your project) is moved, copied or left where it is as the files setting says (moved by default, see Files). --move, --copy and --link override the setting; --keep-source is the same as --copy (a hard link when possible). A file that belongs to another library is copied, not moved. papers list ... --rename runs this command (with --move or --keep-source); the deprecated papers filecheck --rename moves the files, whatever the setting.

docs.title: Control fields when renaming files
docs.text:
$> papers add --move -v --name-template "{AuthorX}{year}-{Title}" --name-title-sep '' --name-author-sep '' esd-4-11-2013
papers: info: found doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013
papers: info: new entry: perrette2013scaling
papers: info: create directory: files/2013
papers: info: mv /home/perrette/playground/papers/esd-4-11-2013.pdf files/PerretteEtAl2013-AScalingApproachToProjectRegionalSeaLevelRiseAndItsUncertainties.pdf
papers: info: renamed file(s): 1

where --name-template is a python template (formatted via the .format() method). Its placeholders are:

  • {author}, {Author}, {AUTHOR}, {authorX}, {AuthorX}: the authors (see below)
  • {year}, {journal} (empty for an entry without journal: a folder of the template that is empty, as in {journal}/{author}, is left out)
  • {title}, {Title}: the title words (see the modifiers below)
  • {key} (or {ID}): the bibtex key of the entry
  • {doi}, {doi_} (the doi with - in place of /, . and the other characters that are not letters or digits, for a file name), {doi_or_id} (the same, or the key if the entry has no doi, or an empty one)

Another placeholder is an error that lists these. A name that would place the file outside the files directory (../{author}) is refused: the files of that entry stay where they are, and papers file rename exits with status 1 once it has renamed the files of the other entries. papers file attach keeps the new link to the file where it is, and exits with status 1.

To rename esd-4-11-2013.pdf as perrette_2013.pdf, the template should be --name-template {author}_{year} --name-author-num 1. If that happens to be the entry key, {key} also works.

To rename esd-4-11-2013.pdf as 2013/Perrette2013-AScalingApproachToProjectRegionalSeaLevelRiseAndItsUncertainties.pdf, name-template should be --name-template {year}/{Author}{year}-{Title} --name-title-sep '' (note the case).

The names made from the template are valid on every system. In each part of the name (the folders and the file name), papers:

  • replaces the characters that Windows does not accept (<>:"|?* and control characters) with - (/ and \ in the field values are replaced with - too, so a field cannot add a folder),
  • removes trailing dots and spaces,
  • adds - after a name that Windows reserves (CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1 to COM9, LPT1 to LPT9),
  • cuts the name to 250 bytes (UTF-8), extension included (a -2 suffix for a name already taken can follow).

This applies only to the names papers makes from the template: a file linked where it is keeps its name, and a file named before this rule keeps its name until the entry is renamed (papers file rename, papers list --rename).

docs.title: Case-sensitive fields
docs.text:
Entries are case-sensitive, and a few more fields are added, so that:

  • author generates perrette
  • Author generates Perrette
  • AUTHOR generates PERRETTE
  • authorX generates perrette, perrette_and_landerer or perrette_et_al depending on the number of authors
  • AuthorX same as authorX but capitalized

The author names, the title words, {doi_} and {doi_or_id} are written in ASCII: accented and non-Latin letters are transliterated with the table of AnyAscii (Müller gives muller, Хрущёв gives khrushchev, 北京 gives beijing), and other characters separate words.

docs.title: Modifiers
docs.text:
The modifiers are:

  • --name-title-sep: separator for title words
  • --name-title-length: max title length, with its separators: the last words are dropped until the title fits, and a first word longer than that is cut
  • --name-title-word-size: min size to be considered a word
  • --name-title-word-num: max number of title words

and similarly:

  • --name-author-sep: separator for authors
  • --name-author-num: number of authors (not relevant for {authorX})

and for entries without author, year or title:

  • --name-unknown-template: the template used instead (default: unknown_{doi_or_id} for file names, {doi_} for keys)
  • --name-unknown-strict: use it only when author, year and title are all missing (by default, when any of them is missing); --no-name-unknown-strict turns off the name.unknown-strict setting for one command

The same template and modifiers system applies to the bibtex key generation by replacing the prefix --name- with --key-, e.g. --key-template.

When the key template gives an empty key (an entry without author, year and DOI, with the default templates), a new entry gets a key from the first word of its title (of at least 3 letters) and its year: only2000 for "Only a title" of 2000, only without year, entry without title. papers check --fix-key and the other renames keep the key of the entry instead.

In the common case where the bibtex (--bibtex), files directory (--filesdir), and name and key formats (e.g. --name-template) do not change, it is convenient to store them in a library configuration (papers init, papers config name.template ...).

docs.title: What a shallow library is
docs.text:
A shallow library has a pool: the path of another library, in its pool setting. It takes its entries from the pool and links to the pool's PDFs. Its file links are those of the pool entries. The entries and PDFs that it adds go to the pool too. The library decides which entries it has: the pool usually has more.

A library without pool is self-contained: it has its own entries and its own PDFs. See Pools for the exchanges between a library and its pool (pull, push, sync).

docs.title: papers init --pool
docs.text:
papers init [DIR] --pool PATH

creates a shallow library that uses the library PATH as pool. PATH must be an existing library without pool of its own (a self-contained library), and not the library itself: papers init --pool PATH and papers config pool PATH stop with an error otherwise, and nothing is created or changed:

$ papers init ~/projects/x --pool ~/projects/thesis
papers: error: --pool ~/projects/thesis: ~/projects/thesis has a pool itself (~/Documents/papers/sealevel): give a library without pool (nothing was changed)

PATH is relative to the current directory, as DIR is: papers init projects/x --pool projects/thesis, run from the home directory, makes ~/projects/thesis the pool of ~/projects/x. The pool path is written in the configuration relative to the library when it is given relative, or when it is under the library (here ../thesis); another path is written with ~ for the home directory, or absolute. papers init --shallow uses the default library as pool (see A global shared library).

A shallow library has no files directory of its own: papers init --pool PATH does not create one.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
In a shallow library, the file links are the pool entry's. The files setting says how a new file gets to the pool:

  • move (the default) and copy: the file is placed in the pool's files directory (moved, or copied: a hard link when possible), named with the pool's name template (a name template set on the library is not used); the library entry and the pool entry link to it there;
  • link: the file stays where it is, and the library entry and the pool entry both link to it there. This works on one machine; on another machine that uses the pool (a pool in a synchronized folder), such links are broken.

What the commands do in a shallow library:

  • add places new files as the files setting says, and adds the new entries to the pool too, whatever the auto-push setting (their origin is recorded, see Origin copies). A change that add makes to the fields of an entry the library has already is pushed only with auto-push;
  • papers file attach and file rename place the files they handle in the same way; file fix copies the files it finds outside the pool into the pool (hard links when possible) and never moves them, unless --move is given for the files of the --search folders;
  • the file links are always pushed, whatever the auto-push setting: a command that changes the files of an entry (file attach, file rename, file detach, file rm, file mv, file fix, edit...) sets the links of the pool entry to match right away, and says so: file links also updated in pool .... The pool entry gets the links that the command added, wherever they point, and the links of the library entry into the pool's files directory, and loses the links that the library entry no longer has. A link that the library entry had before the command, outside the pool's files directory, and that the pool entry does not have (for instance a file of the library's own files/ from when it was self-contained) is not sent; push sends it with the other fields. Only the links change: the other fields are pushed only with auto-push. An entry not shared with the pool gets the links of the pool entry of the same paper updated; if the pool does not have it, the entry is added to the pool, as add does;
  • removing a file and removing an entry are different:
  • papers file detach KEY FILE removes the link from the library entry and from the pool entry; the file stays;
  • papers file rm FILE removes the link from both and deletes the file, unless another entry of the pool or of the library still links to it (kept FILE: an entry of the pool links to it). The PDF is removed for every library that uses the pool;

  • papers rm KEY removes the entry from the library only. The pool entry and its files stay, and papers does not ask about them. papers rm KEY --delete-files (and papers list ... --delete --delete-files) is an error, and nothing is removed:

    $ papers rm perrette_yool2011 --delete-files
papers: error: --delete-files: the files of a shallow library are the pool's: remove them with `papers file rm FILE`

  • pull and sync with the pool link to the pool's files instead of copying them, and the library entry follows the pool entry's links: a link that the pool entry had at the last exchange and no longer has is removed from the library entry (the file is not deleted); push does not send it back to the pool, and the next pull removes it. A link that the pool entry never had stays. The origin copy records the pool entry's links for this, in its file field; an origin copy without it removes nothing until the next exchange;

  • when the pool renames a file, the link breaks. It is repaired by looking the entry up in the pool when the library is loaded (saved on the next write), and by papers file fix. papers file check reports it meanwhile, with the new name (from the pool). A broken link to a file outside the pool is relinked to the pool's file by papers file fix only, and papers file fix --pool PATH also takes the files of the same paper in another library PATH, copied into the pool (see Reconnecting PDFs and a bibtex).

Deleting a file of the pool, with papers file rm in a shallow library or in the pool itself, breaks the links of the other libraries that use it, until their next pull or sync removes the link. papers file check shows the broken link meanwhile. The pool keeps no list of the libraries that depend on it.

A project folder shared with coauthors (git, Dropbox...) should be a self-contained library: the links of a shallow library point into your own pool, which the others do not have. Such a project can still exchange entries with your libraries through --pool PATH (see Exchanges with any library).

A pool can be in a folder synchronized by a cloud client on the local disk (e.g. ~/Dropbox/papers): papers reads and writes the files there, and the client synchronizes them.

docs.title: Changing the pool
docs.text:
papers config pool PATH|none changes the state of a library, and its files follow. When a change copies files or deletes the library's copies, papers lists what it will do and asks Continue? [y/N]; -y answers yes, --dry-run only shows the list, and without a terminal the command stops with the list (pass -y). The files of a pool are never deleted.

Command In a self-contained library In a shallow library papers config pool PATH the library becomes shallow: it links to the copies of its PDFs in PATH, and its own copies are deleted (see below) the library links to the copies of its PDFs in the new pool (see below); the files of the former pool stay where they are papers config pool none (or --unset pool) nothing to do the library becomes self-contained: the pool files that it links to are copied into its files directory (hard links when possible), named with its name template, and the links rewritten; the pool keeps its files

PATH must be an existing library without pool. Each PDF that the library links to must already be linked by the entry of the same paper in PATH: the same file, or a file of the same content. Entries without PDF need not be in PATH, and broken links do not count (papers file fix relinks them afterwards). If an entry has a PDF that PATH does not have, nothing is changed, and the command lists the entries (the first ten, and the number of the others) and the command that copies their PDFs there: papers push --pool PATH KEY..., or papers push --pool PATH --all when there are more than ten.

Otherwise the library links to the copies in PATH. The library's own copies, in its files directory, are deleted, unless an entry of the library or of PATH still links to them; nothing is copied or moved. These commands do not push entries or merge fields: papers push does that. The origin copies of the entries exchanged with PATH before (with --pool PATH) are those of the new pool.

docs.title: From a self-contained project to a shallow one
docs.text:
To move the PDFs of a self-contained library into another library, and make the library shallow:

papers init PATH                # if PATH is not a library yet
papers push --pool PATH --all   # copies the entries and their PDFs to PATH
papers config pool PATH         # links to the copies in PATH, deletes the library's own

For a project with one PDF and the library ~/Documents/papers/arctic:

$ papers config pool ~/Documents/papers/arctic
papers: error: pool ~/Documents/papers/arctic: 1 entry links to PDFs that the pool ~/Documents/papers/arctic does not have (nothing was changed): perrette_landerer2013
Copy them to the pool first: `papers push --pool ~/Documents/papers/arctic perrette_landerer2013`
Then run `papers config pool ~/Documents/papers/arctic` again.
$ papers push --pool ~/Documents/papers/arctic --all
Added -> perrette_landerer2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013, file:1) [to pool ~/Documents/papers/arctic]
$ papers config pool ~/Documents/papers/arctic -y
link to the copies in the pool ~/Documents/papers/arctic for 1 file (same content); the library's copies in files (1 file) are deleted
Modified -> perrette_landerer2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013, file:1)
pool = ~/Documents/papers/arctic (in ~/projects/old-paper/.papers/config.json)
the library is now shallow: it links to the PDFs of the pool entries, and `papers add` adds its new entries to the pool
delete ~/projects/old-paper/files/perrette_et_al_2013_a-scaling-approach-to-project-regional-sea-level-rise-and-its-uncertainties.pdf (hard link: the other links remain)

docs.title: Auto-push
docs.text:
papers config auto-push true in a shallow library makes the commands that change entries push them to the pool: add, edit, tag, list --add-tag and the other actions of list, check, file attach, file rename, file detach, file rm, file mv and file fix. After the command, the entries it changed that are shared with the pool (the pool has the same paper), and the entries new to the library, are pushed as papers push KEY... would push them, files included. The other entries are not pushed: an entry removed from the pool is noted once (see Removed entries). In a self-contained library, the setting has no effect (it has no pool; the libraries of --pool PATH only get what push and sync send).

$ papers config auto-push true
$ papers tag perrette_landerer2013 --add sealevel
Modified -> perrette_landerer2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013, file:1, sealevel) [also modified in pool ~/Documents/papers/sealevel]
  • rm is never pushed: removing an entry from the library does not remove it from the pool.
  • A conflict (the same field changed in the pool since the last exchange) does not stop the command: the entry is saved in the library, is not pushed, and its line says so:
$ papers tag Smith_2020 --add bar
Modified -> Smith_2020: Climate sensitivity revisited (doi:10.1000/abc123, foo | bar) [not pushed: changed in the pool too; papers sync decides]

With auto-push false (the default), nothing is pushed automatically, apart from the new entries of add and the file links (see Files): run papers push or papers sync.

docs.title: Use case: topic libraries
docs.text:
Two topic libraries, each self-contained, and two projects, each shallow on one of them:

  • ~/Documents/papers/sealevel and ~/Documents/papers/arctic: the topic libraries, with the PDFs;
  • ~/projects/thesis: a thesis, shallow on sealevel;
  • ~/projects/arctic-paper: a paper, shallow on arctic.
$ papers init ~/Documents/papers/sealevel
created the library ~/Documents/papers/sealevel
* bibtex:  papers.bib
* files:   files (the files directory of the library)
`papers config` lists and sets the settings
$ papers init ~/Documents/papers/arctic
created the library ~/Documents/papers/arctic
...
$ papers init ~/projects/thesis --pool ~/Documents/papers/sealevel
created the library ~/projects/thesis
* bibtex:  papers.bib
* files:   in the pool (shallow library)
* pool:    ~/Documents/papers/sealevel
`papers config` lists and sets the settings
$ papers init ~/projects/arctic-paper --pool ~/Documents/papers/arctic
created the library ~/projects/arctic-paper
...

Each project adds its papers. They go to its topic library:

$ cd ~/projects/thesis
$ papers add ~/Downloads/esd-4-11-2013.pdf
Added -> perrette_landerer2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013, file:1) [also added to pool ~/Documents/papers/sealevel]
$ cd ~/projects/arctic-paper
$ papers add ~/Downloads/bg-8-515-2011.pdf
Added -> perrette_yool2011: Near-ubiquity of ice-edge blooms in the Arctic (doi:10.5194/bg-8-515-2011, file:1) [also added to pool ~/Documents/papers/arctic]
$ ls ~/projects/arctic-paper ~/Documents/papers/arctic/files
~/Documents/papers/arctic/files:
perrette_et_al_2011_near-ubiquity-of-ice-edge-blooms-in-the-arctic.pdf

~/projects/arctic-paper:
papers.bib

docs.title: A paper relevant to both topics
docs.text:
A shallow library has one pool. The thesis also cites perrette_yool2011, which is in arctic. papers add --pool takes it from arctic, without a query to crossref:

$ cd ~/projects/thesis
$ papers add --pool ~/Documents/papers/arctic --doi 10.5194/bg-8-515-2011
Added -> perrette_yool2011: Near-ubiquity of ice-edge blooms in the Arctic (doi:10.5194/bg-8-515-2011, file:1) [from pool ~/Documents/papers/arctic; also added to pool ~/Documents/papers/sealevel]
$ ls ~/Documents/papers/sealevel/files
perrette_et_al_2011_near-ubiquity-of-ice-edge-blooms-in-the-arctic.pdf
perrette_et_al_2013_a-scaling-approach-to-project-regional-sea-level-rise-and-its-uncertainties.pdf

The entry is now in the thesis and in sealevel. Its PDF is copied into the files directory of sealevel: a hard link when both libraries are on the same disk. papers pull --pool ~/Documents/papers/arctic perrette_yool2011 does the same.

The thesis records an origin copy for arctic. A later change in arctic comes with papers pull --pool, and goes to sealevel with papers push:

$ papers -C ~/Documents/papers/arctic tag perrette_yool2011 --add blooms
Modified -> perrette_yool2011: Near-ubiquity of ice-edge blooms in the Arctic (doi:10.5194/bg-8-515-2011, file:1, blooms)
$ papers pull --pool ~/Documents/papers/arctic
Modified -> perrette_yool2011: Near-ubiquity of ice-edge blooms in the Arctic (doi:10.5194/bg-8-515-2011, file:1, blooms) [from pool ~/Documents/papers/arctic]
$ papers push
Modified -> perrette_yool2011: Near-ubiquity of ice-edge blooms in the Arctic (doi:10.5194/bg-8-515-2011, file:1, blooms) [in pool ~/Documents/papers/sealevel]

The paper project gets the change from its own pool:

$ cd ~/projects/arctic-paper
$ papers status
...
* pool:    ~/Documents/papers/arctic (pool changed)
`papers pull --dry-run` shows the changes, `papers pull` takes them
$ papers pull
Modified -> perrette_yool2011: Near-ubiquity of ice-edge blooms in the Arctic (doi:10.5194/bg-8-515-2011, file:1, blooms) [from pool ~/Documents/papers/arctic]

papers sync --pool ~/Documents/papers/arctic in the thesis also sends the changes made in the thesis to arctic. The two topic libraries can also exchange entries directly, e.g. papers -C ~/Documents/papers/sealevel pull --pool ~/Documents/papers/arctic perrette_yool2011; the thesis then takes the entry from its pool with papers add --doi.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text:
Three ways to use papers with several libraries:

  • a shared files folder (papers 2): several self-contained libraries with a common files directory, and no pool;
  • shallow libraries: projects with a pool;
  • self-contained libraries that exchange entries with --pool PATH.
Shared files folder Shallow libraries Self-contained, --pool PATH Setup papers init --filesdir FOLDER in each project papers init POOL, then papers init --pool POOL in each project papers init in each library Where the PDFs are in the common folder, one copy in the pool's files directory, one copy; the projects link there in each library's files directory; a copy is a hard link when possible Entries each library has its own; a change in one does not reach the other the project chooses which pool entries it has; new entries go to the pool; changes go with push, pull and sync (or auto-push); file links always follow each library has its own; the entries exchanged are kept in step by pull, push and sync with --pool PATH add of a paper another library has reads the PDF again and fetches the entry from crossref (from the cache when the same DOI was fetched on this machine) takes the pool entry, without query; links to the pool's PDF papers add --pool PATH takes the entry and a copy of its files, without query; papers add alone fetches the entry A file renamed the link of the other libraries breaks the links of the other shallow libraries are repaired from the pool, when loaded or by papers file fix each library has its own copy: the others are not affected A file removed the other libraries keep a broken link the PDF is removed for every library of the pool; their next pull or sync removes the link each library removes its own copy only

docs.title: Warnings for a shared files folder
docs.text:
A library configuration of papers 2 has no pool setting: it is read as a self-contained library, as in papers 2. A shared files folder is enough when the libraries are independent and you do not want a shared bibliography. To set it up:

papers init --filesdir ~/Documents/pdfs   # a new library
papers config filesdir ~/Documents/pdfs   # an existing library

Each library only knows its own entries. What to watch for:

  • papers file clean in one library lists the PDFs of the other libraries in the shared folder as unlinked, asks about each, and deletes them once confirmed (all of them with -y). papers file clean --dry-run -y shows the list and deletes nothing.
  • papers rm --delete-files and papers file rm keep a PDF that another entry of the same library links to, but not one that another library links to.
  • papers file rename in one library renames the shared PDF, and the link of the other library breaks. papers file check reports the broken link there. papers file fix --pool OTHER relinks it to the file of the same paper in the other library (copied, a hard link when possible), and papers file fix --search FOLDER if the new name is the one that the library's name template gives the entry (the two libraries use the same template); otherwise attach the renamed file with papers file attach KEY FILE, and remove the link with papers file detach --broken --key KEY.
  • papers push --pool PATH --all then papers config pool PATH in one library deletes the shared PDFs once PATH has copies, and the links of the other library break. Once the other library uses the same pool (papers config pool PATH, which counts the broken links), papers file fix relinks them to the pool's files (see Reconnecting PDFs and a bibtex).

docs.title: Undo and redo
docs.text:
Did a papers add and are unhappy with the result?

papers undo

puts the library back as it was before the command: the bibtex, and the files that the command moved, renamed, copied or deleted. papers redo does the command's changes again. Both take -n N to go several steps at once.

$ papers add ~/Downloads/esd-4-11-2013.pdf --move
$ papers undo
undo: papers.bib restored to 4f1c9a2e papers add ~/Downloads/esd-4-11-2013.pdf --move (2026-10-22 14:03)
    files/perrette_2013_a-scaling-approach.pdf --> moved back to ~/Downloads/esd-4-11-2013.pdf

There is nothing to set up: every command that changes a library records a step in its history.

docs.title: The history
docs.text:
papers history lists the steps of the library, the latest first. > marks where the library is now, and the steps that papers redo can bring back are marked as undone:

$ papers history
  b7e30d51 papers rm smith2020 --delete-files (2026-10-22 14:10)  (undone: `papers redo`)
> 4f1c9a2e papers add ~/Downloads/esd-4-11-2013.pdf --move (2026-10-22 14:03)
  92ad6c07 papers tag smith2020 --add climate (2026-10-21 09:12)
  ...
history: ~/.local/share/papers/history, 3.2 MB (up to 500 MB: the history-size setting; deleted files kept)

A step is named by its identifier, the first column: 8 characters of the sha256 of the step (of its bibtex, its other files, its parent and its time), which never changes. A command that takes a step accepts the start of it, 4 characters or more, as long as no other step starts the same way.

papers restore STEP brings the library to that step. Making a change after an undo starts a new line of history; the undone steps are not lost, and papers restore STEP still reaches them.

docs.title: Taking back an older step
docs.text:
papers undo -n 3 goes back over the last three steps. To take back one step alone and keep the steps made after it, give its identifier (or the start of it, see The history):

$ papers history --revert 92ad
Modified -> smith2020: Sea level rise... (later)

The revert is a new step of the history (papers undo takes it back). For each entry that the step changed, papers compares the entry before the step, after it, and now:

  • an entry that the step added is removed, unless it changed since (it is kept, and a line says so);
  • an entry that the step removed comes back as it was, unless the library has an entry with its key now (or with its key among its former keys): that entry stays, and a line says so when it is not the removed one;
  • a field that the step changed goes back to its value before the step, unless it changed since: then it is a conflict, decided as for papers pull, with --on-duplicate (keep: the value now, update: the value before the step; in a terminal, papers asks);
  • the tags and the file links are taken one by one: those that the step added are removed, those it removed come back, those added since stay;
  • a key that the step changed (with --keep-old-key, which keeps the former key in ids) goes back to the former key.

The files go back as undo moves them, for the files of the step only: a file that the step moved or renamed is moved back, a file it deleted comes back from the history. The pairs that the step recorded in .papers/distinct.json (entries that are not the same paper) are removed. The origin copies (.papers/origin/) are not changed: the next pull or push compares with them, and with auto-push the revert is pushed like any command.

A step that also changed the pool is reverted in the library only; a line gives the command that reverts the pool's step: papers -C ../pool history --revert 3c5e0b7a.

docs.title: Deleted files
docs.text:
A file that a command deletes (papers rm --delete-files, papers file rm, papers file clean...) is kept by the history, and papers undo puts it back, also when no entry linked to it, or when the command was stopped (an error, Ctrl-C) after deleting it:

undo: papers.bib restored to 4f1c9a2e papers add paper.pdf (2026-10-22 14:03)
    files/perrette_2013_a-scaling-approach.pdf: restored from the history

The history keeps up to 500 MB (the history-size setting). Beyond that, the oldest steps are dropped first, and the deleted files that only they needed go to the trash of the system (a step that brought a file back from the history, papers file fix or papers history --revert, needs it too). Before a command that deletes more than the history keeps, or so much that recent steps would be dropped, papers asks first (-y answers yes; without a terminal, the files are kept):

3 files to delete, 812 MB: more than the history keeps (history-size: 500 MB).
- This command cannot be undone: the files go to the trash of the system, not to the history (the history keeps its steps).
Proceed? [y/N]

papers history shows the size of the files each step keeps ([3.2 MB of deleted files]). papers history --drop-files STEP removes from the history the files that the step deleted, and --drop-files PATH the file deleted from PATH (by any step): they go to the trash of the system, the steps stay, and undo says the files are no longer in the history. papers history --remove removes the whole history of the library. Both ask first (-y does not); with --dry-run they only say what they would remove.

If you would rather not keep deleted files at all (you have your own backups, or no space to spare): papers config --global keep-deleted-files false. Deleted files then go straight to the trash of the system, and undo says it cannot bring them back.

docs.title: Changes made outside papers
docs.text:
When you edit the bibtex yourself (in an editor, JabRef, another program, or on another computer that syncs the library), papers notices it at its next command and records your change as a step of its own, "changed outside papers". papers undo never drops it silently: undoing a papers command goes back to what was on disk just before it, your change included.

The step of your change also has the files of .papers/ (the origin records of a library with a pool, distinct.json, files.json) as they were on disk, so a synced folder that brought a new bibtex and new origin records together gives one consistent step. papers notices a change by the bibtex only: a change made outside papers to the files of .papers/ alone is not a step of its own, it becomes part of the next command's step (and undoing that command takes it back too).

Running papers undo right after your own edit undoes that edit (papers redo brings it back). papers restore without a step number does the same: it puts the library back to its last step, as papers left it.

docs.title: Where the history is
docs.text:
The history is kept on your computer, not in the library: ~/.local/share/papers/history on Linux (the history-dir setting). It is not synced or shared with the library: a library you copy to another computer, or receive from someone, starts with an empty history there.

The history follows the library: moving or renaming the library folder keeps it (each library has an identifier, id in .papers/config.json). A copy of a library shares the history up to the copy, then each folder has its own steps. papers export makes a new library, with a history of its own.

papers history --all lists the histories on the computer, with the space each one uses; papers history --remove removes that of the library (--remove ID: another one, e.g. of a library you deleted).

All libraries share one store, so that a file kept by several of them is stored once. papers config history-separate true gives a library a store of its own, with its own history-size.

docs.title: Undo in a library that has a pool
docs.text:
A pool is a library with its own history. A command that exchanges entries with the pool (add in a shallow library, a command that changes entries with auto-push; push, pull, sync) writes both, and each records a step in its own history. When the command wrote the pool, the step of the library also records the step of the pool.

  • papers undo and papers redo in the library undo and redo the pool's step too, as long as the pool is still where the command left it (for redo: where the undo left it). The files that the command moved to the files directory of the pool are moved back.
  • If the pool changed since (another command in the pool or in another library that shares it), papers reverts the pool's step there instead (a new step of the pool, see Taking back an older step). An entry that changed in the pool since stays; in a terminal, papers asks about a field changed on both sides. papers redo then reverts that revert. If the undo took the pool's step back and the pool changed after it, papers redo does the step again there (a new step of the pool, with the same rules).
  • If the pool changed outside papers since its last step, the library only is undone, and a line says so.
  • With auto-push, the shared entries that differ from their origin copy are pushed after the undo or redo, as after any command. In general there is nothing to push: the undo restores the origin copies with the bibtex. There is something when a step was made with auto-push off; that push is then a new step, after which there is nothing to redo, as after any command (papers restore STEP still goes to the steps undone).
  • papers undo --library-only (and redo --library-only) leave the pool as it is: the files that the command moved to the pool are copied back.
  • The pool does not know which libraries use its entries. If another library pulled an entry since the add that undo takes back, that library's link to the PDF breaks: the PDF goes back where it came from, and papers file fix --search FOLDER there finds it.
  • papers -C POOL undo and papers -C POOL redo change the pool only: they undo the last change of the pool, whichever library made it. In the history of the pool, a step made from a library names it: 31 papers add ../new.bib (2026-10-28 10:09, from ~/papers/paper2).
  • The library and the pool are locked during the undo (see Two commands at the same time): no other command changes the pool between the moment undo looks where the pool is and the moment it writes it.
$ papers add ~/Downloads/esd-4-11-2013.pdf --move
$ papers undo
undo: papers.bib restored to 0e8d41f3 papers pull (2026-10-28 10:12)
    ~/sealevel/files/perrette_2013_a-scaling-approach.pdf --> moved back to ~/Downloads/esd-4-11-2013.pdf
pool ../sealevel: also undone, restored to 3c5e0b7a papers push (2026-10-28 10:09)

The library also restores its origin copies (.papers/origin/, see Pools) and .papers/distinct.json to the step it goes back to, and removes those that did not exist at that step. The next exchange then compares the library and the pool to the origin copies of that step:

  • After undoing a pull, or a push whose step the pool did not undo or revert (--library-only, a conflict in the pool), the pool shows as changed in papers status: what the pool has beyond the restored state comes again with the next pull, and the next push does not send the undone state back to the pool.
  • After an undo in the pool, the origin copies of the library still have the newer version, so the pool shows as changed, and a pull takes the pool's older values for the fields the library did not change since. A field that the pool undo removes is a removal in the pool: the pull removes it from the library too, unless the library changed it since (a conflict, see papers pull).

papers restore STEP restores the library only.

docs.title: How undo finds the files
docs.text:
Each step records the files its command moved, renamed, copied or deleted, with their checksum. Undo compares the files that the entries link to now with those of the step it goes back to, and finds each missing file:

  • where the commands in between moved or copied it;
  • by its checksum (.papers/files.json, see Checksums): a file that no entry links to any more is moved, a file that an entry links to, or a file of the pool, is copied;
  • among the deleted files kept by the history.

The rules:

  • A file is never overwritten: if its former place is taken, papers says so and leaves it where it is.
  • A file whose content changed since the command (e.g. a PDF annotated since) is left as it is, with a message.
  • A file outside the library that a command only unlinked (e.g. papers file detach) is never deleted by undo or redo, and the files that no command touched are left alone.
  • In a shallow library, a file that add moved into the files directory of the pool is copied back: the pool entry keeps it.

A file outside the library (~/Downloads, a folder of the project) is recorded with its full path; a file inside it, relative to the library (with the paths absolute setting, with its full path), so that undo in a copy of the library acts on the copy's files.

When another program writes the bibtex while a papers command runs, papers does not overwrite it, and puts back the files that the command had already moved, copied or deleted.

docs.title: Checksums
docs.text: .papers/files.json holds the checksum (sha256) of the files that the entries link to. With the checksums setting (true by default), a command writes the checksum of the files it moves, copies, adds or links. papers file checksum writes the checksums of all the files (or of the entries given), --check reports the files whose content changed since their checksum (e.g. annotated PDFs) and writes nothing. With papers config checksums false, the commands write no checksum, and undo finds the files through the steps of the commands only.

docs.title: What a step holds
docs.text: The bibtex, byte for byte (stored in pieces of about 32 entries: a step that changes one entry adds one piece, a few KB), the files of .papers/ that belong to the library (origin copies, distinct.json, files.json; not config.json), the command and its time, and the files it moved, copied or deleted. The history keeps older contents of the bibtex, but not of the PDFs: an annotated PDF replaces the previous one.

docs.title: Upgrading from papers 2
docs.text:
papers 3 adds the following new functionalities:

  • exchanges between libraries: papers pull, push and sync copy entries from one library to another and keep them in step, with a field-by-field merge (see Pools);
  • shallow libraries: a project library that takes its entries from a shared library, its pool, and links to the pool's PDFs instead of copying them (see Shallow libraries). The shared library can be a library per topic (~/Documents/papers/sealevel), or one library for everything, the default library (see A global shared library);
  • speed: on a library of 10,000 entries, common commands take a third to a half of the time of papers 2 (papers list 0.87 s → 0.27 s, papers add 1.70 s → 0.69 s), and the duplicate checks are two orders of magnitude faster (papers list --duplicates on 1,000 entries: 18.6 s → 0.13 s). Measured with papers 2.19.6 and 3.0.0b4 on the same machine and libraries (scripts/generate_dummy_bib.py);
  • a review of the commands: papers init and papers config replace papers install, the commands on attached files are grouped under papers file, papers list has more actions, and older forms are deprecated (see What else changed);
  • RIS, CSL-JSON and BibJSON: papers add refs.ris (or .json, .bib.json) imports them, papers list --format and papers export write them (see Export);
  • a history of each library, without git: every command is a step; papers undo and papers redo take back any command with the files it moved, renamed or deleted (also outside the library, e.g. a PDF taken from ~/Downloads), a change made outside papers is recorded as a step of its own, and papers history lists the steps. The history is kept on the computer, and git and git-lfs are no longer needed (see Undo and redo). The git backup of papers 2 is no longer used (see Backups of earlier versions);
  • papers status and the pool: a shallow library says whether it is in sync with its pool, or which side changed, and which command shows and exchanges the changes (see Configuration);
  • for programs: --porcelain lists the entries a command added, modified, renamed or removed, and papers edit KEY --from FILE, --set, --unset and --key change an entry without an editor (used by Papers Desktop).

docs.title: What changes for an existing setup
docs.text:
The bibtex files do not change format, and stay readable by papers 2 and by other tools. What changes:

  • The configuration files:
    • the configuration of a project library moves from .papersconfig.json to .papers/config.json the next time papers writes it (also the first command that changes the library, which adds the id of its history). In a project repository, git shows the old file as deleted; scripts that read it need the new path;
    • papers migrate turns the global configuration of papers 2 (~/.config/papersconfig.json on Linux) into the configuration of the global library, and renames it to papersconfig.json.v2.bak. Until then, papers 3 keeps using it outside of libraries, with a warning on every command;
    • papers 2 does not read the new configuration files. To go back to papers 2, restore .papersconfig.json (e.g. from the project repository) or papersconfig.json.v2.bak.

  • Some commands and options are deprecated. They still work, print a warning that names the new form, and are removed in papers 4:

    stop using use instead papers install papers init to create a library, papers config to change it papers filecheck papers file check, papers file fix and the other papers file commands papers list ... --copy papers list ... --rename --keep-source papers list ... --add-files FILE... papers list ... --attach FILE... papers list ... --fetch papers check --fetch --fetch-all --fix-doi --fix-key --format-name KEY..., or papers list ... -K \| papers check --fetch ... - papers doi papers extract --doi-only papers restore-backup papers restore papers backup papers history papers uninstall rm -r .papers, and papers history --remove --attachment --attach -m/--mode --on-duplicate --relative-paths / --absolute-paths papers config paths relative or absolute

    papers git is removed, and the options --git, --no-git, --git-lfs and --restore-files are ignored (papers keeps its history without git, see Undo and redo). papers install --global is removed: it stops with an error, and changes nothing. papers init PATH --global creates the default library, and papers config --global default PATH registers an existing one.

  • papers list keeps its search options and its actions --edit, --delete, --add-tag, --rename (with --keep-source) and --open, and has new ones: --attach, --rm-tag, --detach, --detach-broken, --fix-files, --push, --pull, --sync and --export. Each runs the command it stands for on the listed entries (see Actions on the listed entries). The other commands read the keys listed by papers list -K with -, e.g. papers list --no-file -K | papers check --fetch -y -. A command that reads the keys from a pipe cannot ask questions: answer them with its options, as -y here (see Piping).

  • The output of papers status, papers init and of the exchanges changed: scripts that parse it need updating.

docs.title: What becomes of a papers 2 setup
docs.text: papers 2 papers 3 the global library (papers install --global) the default library, after papers migrate, where it is: a self-contained library that commands run outside of any project act on (papers -C DIR reaches it from anywhere too) a project library (papers install --local) with its own PDFs a self-contained library, the same as a new papers init. papers config pool PATH makes it a shallow library of PATH, once PATH has its PDFs several project libraries with a common filesdir still works (see Comparison). The model preferred in papers 3, which is also more efficient, is a shared library (a pool) and project-bound "shallow" libraries connected to it

docs.title: What happens on the first run
docs.text: papers 3 reads the configuration files of papers 2 as they are. Nothing is converted without a command.

docs.title: The global configuration
docs.text:
The global library of papers 2 is defined by its global configuration (~/.config/papersconfig.json on Linux). papers 3 keeps using it outside of libraries, and prints a warning on every command:

$ papers list
papers: warning: found the global configuration of papers v2 (~/.config/papersconfig.json): it still applies outside of libraries; `papers migrate` turns it into a library, the default library
perrette_landerer2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013, file:1)

papers migrate converts it. In this example the global library of papers 2 is ~/bibliography/papers.bib:

$ papers migrate
global configuration of papers v2: ~/.config/papersconfig.json
  create the library configuration ~/bibliography/.papers/config.json (paths: absolute)
  register ~/bibliography as the default library in ~/.config/papers/config.json
  rename ~/.config/papersconfig.json to ~/.config/papersconfig.json.v2.bak
  • The library gets a configuration file, .papers/config.json in the directory of its bibtex, with the settings of papers 2. It is self-contained: it keeps its own files and has no pool.
  • It is registered as the default library, where it is, unless the global configuration of papers 3 already sets another one: commands run outside of any project act on it (see A global shared library).
  • The bibtex and the PDFs stay where they are. The git backup of papers 2 is no longer used, and stays where it is until you delete it (see Backups of earlier versions). File links stay absolute, as they were; papers migrate --relative makes them relative to the bibtex.
  • papers migrate --dry-run shows what it would do. Running papers migrate a second time does nothing.

papers migrate --folders is a separate step: it moves the files that papers before 2.19 kept in one folder per entry into the files directory. See Migrating from papers 2 for the details.

docs.title: Project libraries
docs.text:
A project library of papers 2 needs no migration. papers 3 reads it as a self-contained library (no pool): its PDFs stay in its own files directory, and it works as in papers 2.

Its configuration file, .papersconfig.json in papers 2, is .papers/config.json in papers 3. papers moves it the next time it writes the configuration (e.g. papers config, or the first command that changes the library, which adds the id of its history), and prints a line that says so:

$ papers config editor vim
moved ~/projects/sealevel/.papersconfig.json to ~/projects/sealevel/.papers/config.json

papers migrate, run in the library, moves it too (--dry-run shows it). A directory that has both files is an error, and papers changes nothing: remove the one you do not want to keep.

It can take papers from another library without changing: papers add --pool ~/Documents/papers --doi DOI takes a paper that ~/Documents/papers has, with a copy of its PDF (a hard link when possible), and papers sync --pool ~/Documents/papers exchanges later changes of the entries taken. Nothing new is written to that library unless you push to it.

docs.title: Sharing papers between projects
docs.text:
The main new use of papers 3: each project keeps its own bibtex, the one its LaTeX document cites, while the PDFs and the curated entries of a topic live once in one library. A new project on the same topic takes the entries and PDFs it needs from there, without fetching anything or storing a PDF twice. A correction made in one project reaches the others with papers sync.

An existing project library can be that library as it is: a new project uses it as pool.

cd ~/projects/tides
papers init --pool ../sealevel           # a shallow library
papers add --doi 10.5194/esd-4-11-2013   # taken from ../sealevel, with its PDF
papers pull perrette_yool2011            # or by key
papers sync                              # later: exchange the changes both ways

To move the PDFs of an existing project into a library of the topic, and make the project shallow:

cd ~/projects/sealevel
papers init ~/Documents/papers/sealevel                # a new self-contained library
papers push --pool ~/Documents/papers/sealevel --all   # copies the entries and their PDFs there
papers config pool ~/Documents/papers/sealevel         # link to its PDFs, delete the project's copies

papers push --pool PATH requires PATH to be a library already (papers init PATH creates it). It copies the PDFs as hard links when possible, so the PDFs are not read again and nothing is fetched. papers config pool PATH refuses until PATH has every PDF of the library, and then names the entries to push.

The Quickstart runs through a self-contained project and a shallow project with their output, Shallow libraries describes shallow libraries, and Pools describes the exchanges.

docs.title: What else changed
docs.text:
• papers init asks no questions, and fails if the folder has a library already (use papers config). By default it creates a self-contained library, which keeps its own PDFs, as in papers 2; papers init --pool PATH creates a shallow library.
  • papers config gets and sets the settings, in the style of git config (see Configuration).
  • The global configuration of papers 3 is ~/.config/papers/config.json on Linux. It holds default settings, and optionally the default library (papers config --global default PATH).
  • The files setting (move by default, copy, link or ask) applies to papers file rename too, and ask asks for each file (see Files).
  • papers file groups the commands on attached files: attach, detach, rm, mv, rename, check, fix, clean (see Files).
